25258 explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md
     1	<!-- What a fresh Opus session believes about Fortress from its pre-training alone, asked on 2026-10-08 at the curator's idea, run as `claude -p` outside the repository with no tools: the prompt and the answer, verbatim. The input to the skills distillation audit, which grades each claim against the record. -->
     2	
     3	# Fortress from pre-training: the quiz
     4	
     5	## The prompt
     6	
     7	> From your own knowledge only, without any tool or search, describe the Fortress programming language that Sun Microsystems Labs designed (2003 to 2012). Write for a programmer who knows Java, Scala, Haskell and Julia and is about to work on Fortress's interpreter, compiler and standard library.
     8	> 
     9	> Cover each of these, and mark every statement with your confidence (sure, likely, guess):
    10	> 1. Why the language exists and what its designers aimed for.
    11	> 2. The type system: traits, objects, generics and static parameters (type, nat, int, bool, opr), variance, exclusion and `comprises`.
    12	> 3. Dispatch and overloading: how a call chooses among declarations, at compile time and at run time.
    13	> 4. Parallelism: which constructs run in parallel by default, `for` loops, tuples, `also`, `atomic`, work stealing, `spawn`.
    14	> 5. Syntax and notation: juxtaposition, operators, Unicode, the mathematical rendering, how a program looks.
    15	> 6. Numbers: the numeric types, literals, overflow, coercions.
    16	> 7. The standard library: arrays, ranges, generators, reductions (`SUM`, `BIG`), its algebraic traits.
    17	> 8. Components and APIs.
    18	> 9. How the implementation was built: interpreter, compiler, target platform.
    19	> 10. The traps: where a programmer who knows the four languages above would most likely assume something wrong about Fortress.
    20	
    21	## The answer
    22	
    23	# Fortress: a briefing from memory
    24	
    25	Everything below comes from memory, with no sources checked. Each statement carries a tag: **[sure]**, **[likely]** or **[guess]**. Treat **[guess]** items as things to look up. Where the spec and the implementation disagree, the source tree is the authority. Large parts of the spec were never implemented, or were implemented only in part.
    26	
    27	---
    28	
    29	## 1. Why the language exists and what its designers aimed for
    30	
    31	- Guy Steele led the design in the Programming Language Research group at Sun Labs. **[sure]** Eric Allen, David Chase, Victor Luchangco, Jan-Willem Maessen and Sukyoung Ryu were core contributors, and Sam Tobin-Hochstadt was among the others involved at various points. **[likely]**
    32	- It began under DARPA's HPCS (High Productivity Computing Systems) program, alongside Cray's Chapel and IBM's X10. **[sure]** Sun was not funded for the program's final phase, around 2006, but kept the project going as open-source research. **[likely]**
    33	- Its slogan was "to do for Fortran what Java did for C." **[sure]** The name is often explained as a play on "secure Fortran." **[likely]**
    34	- The design goals were: **[sure]**
    35	  - Code that looks like mathematical notation, so a whiteboard formula and the program are nearly the same.
    36	  - Implicit parallelism by default, so the programmer must opt into sequential execution rather than into parallel execution.
    37	  - A "growable" language, in the spirit of Steele's *Growing a Language* talk. The core stays small, and most features (numbers, arrays, even many operators and reductions) live in libraries written in Fortress.
    38	  - A strong static type system with multiple inheritance of traits and symmetric multiple dispatch.
    39	- Version 1.0 of the specification appeared around 2008. **[likely]** Oracle acquired Sun in 2010. Steele announced in 2012 that active development was winding down. **[sure]** The stated reason was roughly that the hard remaining problems were implementing the type system (generic multiple dispatch with reified types) efficiently on the JVM, and that those problems were not worth more investment. **[likely]**
    40	
    41	## 2. The type system
    42	
    43	- **Traits** are the unit of inheritance. **[sure]**
    44	  - A trait may declare abstract and concrete methods, including bodies. **[sure]**
    45	  - A trait has no fields, though it can declare abstract getters. **[likely]**
    46	  - Multiple inheritance of traits is allowed: `trait T extends {A, B} ... end`. **[sure]**
    47	- **Objects** are the concrete, instantiable types. **[sure]**
    48	  - An object is a leaf. Nothing can extend an object. **[sure]**
    49	  - An object is either a singleton (`object Empty extends List end`) or parameterized by its fields, which also serve as the constructor: `object Cons[\T\](first: T, rest: List[\T\]) extends List[\T\] ... end`. **[sure]**
    50	  - Fields are immutable unless declared `var` or `settable`. **[likely]**
    51	- **Generic (static) parameters** are written `[\ ... \]` in ASCII and render as ⟦ ⟧ (white square brackets). **[sure]** The kinds are:
    52	  - Types (plain names, optionally with `extends` bounds). **[sure]**
    53	  - `nat n`, `int i` and `bool b`: compile-time values used in types such as fixed-size vectors and arrays. **[sure]**
    54	  - `opr ⊕`: an operator passed as a parameter. Algebraic traits such as `Monoid[\T, ⊕\]` use this to name *which* operation forms the monoid. **[sure]**
    55	  - `dim` and `unit`, for physical dimensions. **[likely]**
    56	  - Extra constraints go in `where { ... }` clauses. **[sure]** Where clauses can also introduce additional type variables, a form of bounded existential or hidden parameter. **[likely]**
    57	- **Variance:** generic types are invariant, and there is no declaration-site `+T` or `-T` as in Scala. **[likely]** Covariant-style APIs are approximated with extra type parameters and `where` constraints. **[guess]**
    58	- **Exclusion** has two forms. **[sure]**
    59	  - `excludes { U, V }` asserts that no type is a subtype of both.
    60	  - `comprises { A, B, C }` declares that every subtype of the trait is a subtype of one of the listed types. It is like Scala's `sealed`, but stated in the type. `comprises { ... }` with an ellipsis exists for hidden or private subtypes. **[likely]**
    61	  - Distinct object types exclude each other automatically, because objects are leaves. **[sure]**
    62	  - Exclusion exists mainly so the overloading checker can prove that two declarations never both apply (see §3). Without exclusion, many reasonable overload sets would be rejected as possibly ambiguous. **[sure]**
    63	- **Tuples, arrows and the top type** are structural and somewhat special.
    64	  - Arrow types are written `A -> B`, and a function can declare `throws`. **[sure]**
    65	  - `()` is the unit/void type. **[sure]**
    66	  - Tuple types are not ordinary trait types. I believe `Any` does not include tuples, so tuples cannot be stored as `Any` like an ordinary value. **[guess]**
    67	- **Contracts** can appear on declarations: `requires`, `ensures` and `invariant`. `property` declarations state algebraic laws, and `test` declarations are their checkable counterpart. **[likely]**
    68	
    69	## 3. Dispatch and overloading
    70	
    71	- Fortress uses symmetric multiple dispatch. A call chooses among overloaded declarations using the **run-time types of all arguments**, not just the receiver. **[sure]** It is close to Julia in spirit, unlike Java's static overloading.
    72	- **Compile time:** **[likely]**
    73	  - The static argument types determine the set of declarations that are applicable and accessible.
    74	  - The type checker assigns the call a static return type from the most specific *statically* applicable declaration.
    75	- **Run time:** among declarations applicable to the dynamic argument types, the most specific is chosen. **[sure]**
    76	- **Overload-set validity is checked statically, per pair of declarations**, so no run-time ambiguity can occur. **[sure]** For any two overloads of the same name, one of these must hold:
    77	  1. The parameter types exclude each other, so they can never both apply. **[sure]**
    78	  2. One declaration is strictly more specific than the other. **[sure]**
    79	  3. **The meet rule:** a third declaration exists whose parameter type is the intersection of the two, which resolves the overlap. **[sure]**
    80	- **Return-type rule:** if declaration A is more specific than B, then A's return type must be a subtype of B's. This keeps the static type sound under dynamic dispatch. **[sure]**
    81	- Making all of this modular with generics and multiple inheritance was a research problem in itself. There were papers by Allen, Hilburn, Ryu, Steele and others around 2009 to 2011, for example at OOPSLA, on type-checking modular multiple dispatch with parametric polymorphism. **[sure]** Generic overloads need instance-level reasoning: specificity is compared over all instantiations. **[likely]**
    82	- **Functional methods:** a method declared in a trait with `self` in a parameter position is called as a top-level function, `f(x, y)`, not `x.f(y)`. It takes part in overloading with top-level functions of the same name and dispatches on the position where `self` appears. **[sure]** Most operators are defined this way, for example `opr +(self, other: T): T` inside a trait. **[likely]**
    83	- **Dotted methods**, `x.m(y)`, dispatch on the receiver and then overload on the other arguments in the usual way. **[likely]**
    84	- Dispatch on generic type arguments requires reified types at run time, which the JVM does not provide. Erasure was a major implementation pain. **[likely]**
    85	
    86	## 4. Parallelism
    87	
    88	- The defaults are parallel. **[sure]**
    89	  - **Tuple components are evaluated in parallel**: `(f(x), g(y))`. **[sure]**
    90	  - **Function arguments are evaluated in parallel**, because an argument list is a tuple. **[sure]**
    91	  - **Operands of binary operators** may be evaluated in parallel. **[likely]**
    92	  - **`for` loops are parallel by default.** Iteration order is determined by the generator, and iterations may run concurrently. **[sure]**
    93	  - **Comprehensions and reductions** (`SUM`, `BIG op`) are parallel by default. **[sure]**
    94	- What is sequential: **[sure]**
    95	  - Statements in a `do ... end` block, separated by newlines or `;`.
    96	  - A sequential loop is written by wrapping the generator: `for i <- seq(1:n) do ... end`. **[sure]** There is also `while`. **[sure]**
    97	- **Generators** are `x <- expr`, where `expr` is a `Generator[\T\]` such as a range, array or set. **[sure]**
    98	  - A loop or comprehension can combine several generators and Boolean filters, separated by commas: `for i <- 1:n, j <- 1:m, i ≠ j do ... end`. **[sure]**
    99	  - Library code implements a generator through a `generate` method that takes a reduction and a body function. This is how parallel splitting becomes a library decision rather than a compiler decision. **[likely]** I believe the signature is roughly `generate[\R\](r: Reduction[\R\], body: T -> R): R`. **[guess]**
   100	- **`also`** creates explicit parallel blocks: `do A also do B also do C end`. **[sure]**
   101	- **`spawn e`** creates an explicit thread object. Its result is read with `.val()` or `.wait()`. **[likely]** The exact method names are **[guess]**.
   102	- **`atomic e`** executes `e` as a transaction (transactional memory semantics). `tryatomic` fails instead of retrying. **[sure]** In the interpreter, transactions came from a software TM implementation in Java. I believe it was descended from DSTM2 or similar Sun Labs work. **[guess]**
   103	- **Locality and distribution:** the spec has regions (a tree describing the machine), distributions for arrays, and `at r do ... end` to place computation. **[likely]** These were mostly unimplemented beyond stubs, or only on a shared-memory interpreter. **[likely]**
   104	- **Scheduling** is work stealing. The interpreter ran tasks on a fork/join pool derived from Doug Lea's jsr166y (the precursor of `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). **[likely]**
   105	- **Data races are the programmer's problem.** A plain `var` mutated from a parallel `for` loop is racy. Use reductions, `atomic`, or reduction variables. **[sure]** I believe the spec defines "reduction variables": a variable assigned with `+=` inside a loop is treated as a reduction. **[guess]**
   106	
   107	## 5. Syntax and notation
   108	
   109	- **Two forms of the same program** **[sure]**
   110	  - Source is plain text, either ASCII or Unicode.
   111	  - A tool called **Fortify** renders source as LaTeX for mathematical typesetting.
   112	  - ASCII names map to symbols. For example, `ZZ32` renders as ℤ32, `SUM` as Σ, `[\ \]` as ⟦ ⟧, `<-` as ←, `->` as →, and `NOT` as ¬. **[sure]**
   113	  - You can type the Unicode characters directly instead. **[sure]**
   114	- **Rendering conventions:** **[likely]**
   115	  - All-caps or doubled-letter type names (`ZZ`, `RR`, `QQ`) render in blackboard bold.
   116	  - A trailing `_x` becomes a subscript.
   117	  - Identifiers in certain case styles render in italic, roman or bold.
   118	- **Delimiters are keywords**, not braces: `do ... end`, `if c then ... elif ... else ... end`, `object ... end`, `trait ... end`, `case ... of ... end`, `typecase`, `label ... end` with `exit`. **[likely]**
   119	- **Comments** are `(* ... *)` and nest. **[sure]**
   120	- **Declarations:** **[sure]**
   121	  - `x = 3` is an immutable binding. **[sure]**
   122	  - `var x: ZZ32 = 3` declares a mutable variable. **[likely]** A related form, `x: ZZ32 := 3`, declares a mutable variable with an initializer. **[likely]**
   123	  - `x := e` is assignment. **[sure]** Compound forms such as `+=` exist. **[likely]**
   124	  - `f(x: ZZ32): ZZ32 = x + 1` declares a function. **[sure]**
   125	  - `opr` declares operators: prefix, infix, postfix, and bracket pairs such as `opr |x|`, `⌊x⌋` and `‖v‖`. **[sure]**
   126	- **Juxtaposition** **[sure]**
   127	  - `f x`, `2 x` and `a b` are meaningful, and the meaning depends on types.
   128	  - If the left operand is a function, juxtaposition is **application**.
   129	  - Otherwise it is the **juxtaposition operator**, which is overloadable. On numbers it means multiplication. On strings it means concatenation. **[likely]**
   130	  - Tight versus loose juxtaposition, and the whitespace around it, affects grouping. For example, `sin x y` and `a b+c` versus `a b + c` can parse differently. **[likely]**
   131	- **Whitespace is significant around operators** **[sure]**
   132	  - `a - b` is infix, and `a -b` is application of a prefix `-`, or an error.
   133	  - Infix operators must have symmetric whitespace.
   134	  - `a[i]` is subscripting, while `a [i]` can mean juxtaposition with a one-element array.
   135	  - Newlines can end expressions. A line that starts with an infix operator continues the previous line, but a trailing operator is the safe way to continue. **[likely]**
   136	- **Precedence is not a total order** **[sure]**
   137	  - Only "mathematically conventional" pairs have a defined precedence. Mixing unrelated operators without parentheses is a **static error**; I believe `a ∧ b ∨ c` is rejected. **[likely]**
   138	- **Chained comparisons** such as `a < b ≤ c` mean the conjunction of `a < b` and `b ≤ c`. **[sure]**
   139	- **Syntax extension:** libraries could add new syntax through grammar declarations, which hooked into the parser. **[likely]** It was hygienic and macro-like, built on Rats!-style grammar productions. **[guess]**
   140	
   141	A small sketch (approximate):
   142	
   143	```
   144	component Hello
   145	export Executable
   146	run() = println "Hello, World!"
   147	end
   148	```
   149	
   150	## 6. Numbers
   151	
   152	- **Integers** **[sure]**
   153	  - `ZZ32` and `ZZ64` (ℤ32, ℤ64) are fixed-width.
   154	  - `ZZ` is arbitrary precision. **[likely]**
   155	  - `NN32` and `NN64` are naturals. **[likely]**
   156	  - `IntLiteral` is the type of integer literals. **[likely]**
   157	- **Other numeric types**
   158	  - `RR32` and `RR64` are floating point. **[sure]**
   159	  - `QQ` holds rationals. **[likely]**
   160	  - `CC` (complex) is in the spec, and the library implementation was partial. **[likely]**
   161	  - Interval arithmetic was mentioned in the spec. **[guess]**
   162	- **Literals** have their own types and coerce to the context's type. Integer literals have type `IntLiteral` and float literals have type `FloatLiteral`. This allows `x: RR64 = 3`. **[likely]**
   163	  - Radix is written as a subscript: `1010_2`, `FF_16`. **[likely]**
   164	  - Digit grouping exists in the spec. I don't remember the separator. **[guess]**
   165	- **Overflow:** fixed-width integer overflow **throws an exception** rather than wrapping. **[likely]** Some wrapping or modular types may have existed separately. **[guess]**
   166	- **Coercion** **[likely]**
   167	  - Implicit conversions are user-definable through `coerce` declarations in the target type.
   168	  - The spec has detailed rules for resolving coercion against overloading, which essentially prefer no coercion to coercion.
   169	  - The interpreter implemented a subset of these rules. **[guess]**
   170	- **Dimensions and units** **[likely]**
   171	  - Physical dimensions and units were part of the type system in the spec: `dim Length`, `unit meter m`, values like `3 m/s`, and conversion with `in`.
   172	  - The reference implementation largely omitted them, and they were later cut back. **[likely]**
   173	
   174	## 7. The standard library
   175	
   176	- **Library-first design:** much of the language is written in Fortress library code. **[sure]**
   177	  - The main files are `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin` (`.fsi` and `.fss`). **[likely]**
   178	  - Primitives call Java through a native or builtin-primitive mechanism, so many library operators bottom out in Java classes. **[likely]**
   179	- **Ranges** **[sure]**
   180	  - `a:b` is a closed range.
   181	  - `a#n` is a range that starts at `a` and has `n` elements.
   182	  - Strided and open forms exist.
   183	  - Ranges are generators.
   184	- **Arrays** **[likely]**
   185	  - `Array[\T, E\]` is the general type. `Array1`, `Array2` and `Array3` are specializations with static `nat` bounds and sizes.
   186	  - Vectors and matrices (`Vector[\T, n\]`, `Matrix[\T, m, n\]`) carry sizes in the type.
   187	  - Array literals use whitespace for columns and newlines or `;` for rows, as in `[1 2 3]`. **[likely]**
   188	  - Default indexing is 0-based. **[likely]** Indexing is `a[i]` and `a[i, j]`. **[sure]**
   189	  - Mutable and immutable arrays both exist.
   190	- **Collections** **[likely]**
   191	  - Lists, sets, maps and multisets exist as persistent or functional structures.
   192	  - Some are implemented as balanced trees with parallel generators.
   193	  - Strings were rope-like and built from concatenation nodes, so juxtaposition concatenation is cheap. **[guess]**
   194	- **Reductions and comprehensions** **[sure]**
   195	  - `SUM[i <- 1:n] a[i]` and `PROD[...]` are reductions.
   196	  - `BIG op [gen] body` reduces with any operator that has a big form. You declare one with `opr BIG ⊕ ...`. **[likely]**
   197	  - Comprehensions build collections: `{ x^2 | x <- S, x > 0 }`, `⟨ ... ⟩` for lists, and `[ ... ]` for arrays. **[likely]**
   198	- **The `Reduction` abstraction** has an empty element, a `join`, and possibly `lift` and `unlift`. Generators are parameterized over it, so one generator implementation serves all reductions. **[likely]**
   199	- **Algebraic traits** **[sure]**
   200	  - The library has a hierarchy parameterized by operator: `Associative[\T, ⊕\]`, `Commutative`, `Identity`, `Monoid[\T, ⊕\]`, `CommutativeMonoid`, `Group`, `Ring` and `Field`, plus ordering traits such as `PartialOrder` and `TotalOrder`. **[likely]**
   201	  - These traits are what make `BIG ⊕` reductions legitimately parallel. Associativity is *declared*, through `property` declarations, rather than proved. **[likely]**
   202	
   203	## 8. Components and APIs
   204	
   205	- **The two module kinds** **[sure]**
   206	  - An **API** (file extension `.fsi`) contains only declarations, like an interface for a module.
   207	  - A **component** (file extension `.fss`) contains implementations.
   208	  - A component `export`s one or more APIs and `import`s others: `import List.{...}`, `import Foo.{bar, baz}`, and `import api Foo`. **[likely]**
   209	  - A component's code may see only imported APIs, never other components directly. **[sure]**
   210	- **Linking** **[likely]**
   211	  - Components are linked into compound components by matching exports to imports.
   212	  - An `upgrade` operation replaces a component inside a compound one.
   213	  - The spec envisions a persistent, transactional "fortress" store that holds compiled components.
   214	- **The main program** exports `Executable` and defines `run()`. **[sure]** Early versions took `run(args: String...)`. **[guess]**
   215	- **Implementation** **[likely]**
   216	  - The interpreter implemented a simplified version: API and component files found on a path, one component per file, and imports resolved by name.
   217	  - The store and upgrade machinery were mostly not implemented.
   218	
   219	## 9. How the implementation was built
   220	
   221	- **Language and hosting** **[sure]**
   222	  - Everything was written in **Java**, and targeted the JVM.
   223	  - It was open source under a BSD-style license. It was hosted first on Sun infrastructure (sunsource.net / projectfortress) and later mirrored elsewhere. **[likely]**
   224	- **Front end** **[likely]**
   225	  - The parser was generated with **Rats!** (from Robert Grimm's xtc). It is a PEG/packrat parser, which suits whitespace-sensitive and extensible syntax.
   226	  - AST classes were generated from a declarative description by a tool called **ASTGen**. **[likely]**
   227	  - Some parts were written in Scala later in the project. **[likely]** I believe the type checker and some compiler phases were among them. **[guess]**
   228	- **Static phases** **[likely]**
   229	  - Disambiguation (names versus juxtaposition versus application), operator-precedence resolution, desugaring (generators, reductions and comprehensions into `generate` calls), and type checking with the overloading-validity checker.
   230	  - For long stretches, the interpreter ran with static type checking incomplete or off by default. Dispatch relied on dynamic checks. **[likely]**
   231	- **Interpreter** **[sure]**
   232	  - A tree-walking interpreter over the AST.
   233	  - Parallelism ran on fork/join work stealing. **[likely]**
   234	  - Run with something like `fortress run Foo.fss`. **[likely]**
   235	- **Compiler** **[likely]**
   236	  - Later work, around 2009 to 2012, compiled Fortress to **JVM bytecode** using ASM.
   237	  - It covered a subset of the language and specialized generics by instantiation, to work around erasure. **[guess]**
   238	  - The project ended before the compiler covered the whole language. **[likely]**
   239	- **Test suite:** a large directory of `.fss` test programs with expected output was used as the regression suite. **[likely]**
   240	
   241	## 10. The traps
   242	
   243	1. **Arguments, tuples and loops run in parallel.** **[sure]** `f(print "a", print "b")` has no defined order. A `for` loop that does `acc := acc + x` is a data race. Use `SUM`, a `BIG` reduction, `seq(...)` or `atomic`. Java habits will break things here.
   244	2. **Juxtaposition is not just function application.** **[sure]** Coming from Haskell, `f x` looks familiar, but `2 x` multiplies, `"a" "b"` concatenates, and the meaning depends on the left operand's type. Also, `f x y` does not curry as in Haskell. **[likely]**
   245	3. **Whitespace changes the parse.** **[sure]** `a -b`, `a[i]` versus `a [i]`, and unbalanced spacing around infix operators all matter. Scala and Java programmers assume whitespace is insignificant.
   246	4. **No global precedence table.** **[sure]** Parenthesize when mixing operators that are not conventionally related. Chained comparisons are conjunctions, not `(a < b) < c`.
   247	5. **Overloading is dynamic multiple dispatch.** **[sure]** This is unlike Java, where overloads are chosen statically. It is like Julia, but **the compiler statically rejects overload sets that could be ambiguous**, whereas Julia raises an ambiguity error only at run time. Expect to add meet declarations or `excludes` and `comprises` to get overload sets accepted.
   248	6. **Functional methods.** **[sure]** A method in a trait with `self` as a parameter is called as `f(x)`, not `x.f()`, and it overloads with top-level functions.
   249	7. **Objects are final and traits have no fields.** **[sure]** Scala users will look for class inheritance or abstract classes with state. There are none.
   250	8. **Generics are invariant**, with no Scala-style `+T` or `-T`. **[likely]** Type parameters are written `[\T\]`, not `[T]`, and `[...]` is indexing.
   251	9. **`=` binds and `:=` assigns.** **[sure]** `x = 5` is an immutable declaration, not an assignment. Writing it on an existing variable is a redeclaration or an error.
   252	10. **Evaluation is strict, not lazy.** **[sure]** Haskell's laziness and purity are absent. Mutation and effects are common, and laziness exists only inside generators by convention.
   253	11. **Fixed-width integers throw on overflow** instead of wrapping as in Java. **[likely]** Literals are not `int` or `Int`: they have literal types that coerce from context. **[likely]**
   254	12. **The spec and the implementation differ.** **[sure]** Dimensions and units, distributions and regions, full coercion rules, the component store and `upgrade` are in the spec but are absent or partial in the code. Check the tests and library source before trusting the spec.
   255	13. **The interpreter can be more permissive than the spec.** **[likely]** Code that runs under the interpreter may not pass the full type checker or the compiler. Don't treat "it runs" as "it's well typed."
   256	14. **The library defines the "language."** **[sure]** Many things that look built in, such as `+` on `ZZ32`, `SUM`, ranges and even some control-like constructs, live in `FortressLibrary`/`FortressBuiltin` and in Java primitives. Changing them means changing library code, and sometimes the Java primitive behind it, not the parser.
   257	
   258	**What to verify first:** the exact concrete syntax for variable declarations, the details of `spawn` and reduction variables, the digit-separator syntax, and which phases run in the current build (type checker on or off, interpreter or compiler path).

1	<!-- The territory map, assembled 2026-09-16 by the coordinating session from the survey reports in this directory, before the historical source tree was opened for modification. The surveys are the evidence of that day; sections 0, 2 and 7 describe the tree as it stands, section 6 the development loop, and the order of work and the open decisions are in coordinator/PLAN.md, to which sections 4 and 5 point. Every claim cites a survey section, a file:line, a commit, or a FACTS or POSITIONS entry. Read after FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md; it does not repeat them. -->
     2	
     3	# The territory map
     4	
     5	## 0. Terms used here
     6	
     7	Path: one of the two execution routes, the interpreter (`fortress <file>.fss`, "walk") or the compiler (`fortress compile` then `fortress run`); "both paths" means the shared front end.
     8	
     9	World: which prelude a run links against; the interpreter world is `FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin` + `AnyType`, the compiler world is `CompilerLibrary` + `CompilerBuiltin` + `CompilerAlgebra` + `AnyType` (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:114-139`, `CompilerAlgebra` since `1bd8d3ad1`; `modules-and-phases.md` B.13).
    10	
    11	Prelude: the library a world loads without an import; the compiler world's four components are 2,405 lines against the interpreter world's 5,314 (`wc -l` of the `.fss`; `spec-to-implementation.md` §2 names the files).
    12	
    13	Switch-over: phase 4 of `coordinator/PLAN.md`, where the compiled path starts reading the interpreter's library and the compiler's own three prelude files are deleted, their tests kept (POSITIONS 2026-09-21, the library route); until then each path links its own world.
    14	
    15	Gate: what a change must pass to land: on a clean build, `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem` at zero failures, thirteen compiled `atomic` programs three times at four threads, the ladder regression (85 files compiled and run against their baseline, the eighteen microGPT components compiled only) and the checker count, the compiled checker's errors over the interpreter's library, reported and never red on its own (protocol, hard rules; `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`). Counts here are from climb batch 5's follow-up D gate (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-5/followup-D/gate/summary.txt`); the current ones are in the last landed `climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt`.
    16	
    17	Shadow: a prototype of an edit to the original tree, made by compiling edited copies of the files and putting their class files ahead of the real ones on the classpath; no tracked file changes, and the gate cannot see it (`perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh`; FACTS "The `nat` plan's minimal design works as a shadow").
    18	
    19	Sealed tree: the original tree, everything outside `explorations/` and `research/`; sealed through `75cca6683` (POSITIONS 2026-09-17), editable since, each edit test first and flagged at commit (protocol, hard rules).
    20	
    21	## 1. The five surveys, and the walkthrough beside them
    22	
    23	`modules-and-phases.md`: the 22 packages with sizes, the import graph, the dead modules, the two pipelines phase by phase, the cache, the runtime, native interop, and the one-table divergence of the paths (B.14).
    24	
    25	`spec-to-implementation.md`: the 53 chapters of the July 2012 draft, a table of about 110 features with the parser rule, checker class, interpreter, codegen and prelude location of each, and the layered picture of the numeric tower (§4).
    26	
    27	`test-coverage.md`: the census of every test corpus and JUnit class, what the 1,377 and 382 are made of, the two corpora that never meet, the blind spots by module, and the loop timings.
    28	
    29	`dormant-code.md` (part five, added at Pavol's request): the census of what is present, carries a design, and does not run: commented-out library declarations and `Library/incomplete/`, commented-out visitors and off-by-default flags in the source, commented-out test halves and the aspirational directories, the spec's genuinely dormant text and its 62 "not yet supported" notes, the papers; each item judged finished-unwired, sketch, superseded or unknown, and tied to a path step.
    30	
    31	`design-intent-sources.md`: the five places rationale is written (in-repo papers, the Steele corpus, our extracts, the spec's draft-only notes and Internal Document, source comments and commits), and a table by design area of what intent the spec leaves unstated.
    32	
    33	`compile-path-walkthrough.md` (part six, written 2026-09-20 for the checker decisions): the compile path followed end to end, one section per stage — parsing, name resolution and grammar expansion, the checker (what it walks, what it writes, its counts on the library before climb batch 4), the desugaring switches that make the paths differ, code generation, the second JVM and the stamping class loader, native bindings in both worlds, `nat`, and a glossary.
    34	
    35	## 2. The shape of the system, in thirteen facts
    36	
    37	The editable surface is about 149,000 hand-written Java lines and 19,900 Scala lines; the other 535,000 Java lines are generated and checked in (counted as in `modules-and-phases.md` A.1).
    38	
    39	The AST in `nodes/` is the only intermediate representation from parse to bytecode; there is no lower IR and no optimizing middle (B.1).
    40	
    41	The two paths run the same first four phases (pre-disambiguation desugaring, disambiguation, grammar rewriting of apis, pre-typecheck desugaring) under different switches: the compiler world bounds every unbounded static parameter by `Object` in phase 1 and walk turns off the three desugarings gated on `use_scala` (`Shell.java:268-286`, `:371-386`, `:422`); the compiler adds integer-literal folding and codegen; the interpreter's type-check phase is present but inert because the flag defaults off (B.1, `Shell.java:1275`).
    42	
    43	`fortress compile` and `fortress run` are two JVMs with two classpaths; `run` never enters `Shell.java` (B.0).
    44	
    45	A user grammar is expanded before phase 1 runs on the component, by a Rats! run plus a javac run in a temp directory per compile; the GRAMMAR phase in the phase array touches apis only (B.3).
    46	
    47	Generics are compiled once as template bytecode and stamped out by name rewriting in `InstantiatingClassloader` at class-load time, a size stamped into the class name and, where it is read as a value, substituted as its numeral; instantiation renames, it does not change representation (B.11; FACTS "A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`").
    48	
    49	The api cache key is a hash of the source directory path, not of content; staleness is decided by file dates alone (B.10).
    50	
    51	Tasks and transactions exist twice, once in `interpreter/evaluator/` and once in `runtimeSystem/`, independent implementations of the same two ideas (B.11); a fix in one is not a fix in the other.
    52	
    53	The number tower is flat in both worlds. In the one library, since climb batch 6 rung F (`d846e3644`), `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each carrying its own algebra, each wider type converting from each narrower one by `coerce` (into `RR64` from `ZZ32` alone), and `Number` declares only `asFloat` and one numeric `=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:276-606`; FACTS "The one library's number tower is flat"); the compiler prelude has been flat since 2009 (`6896886fb`), its `Number` empty and no algebraic trait above it (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:96`).
    54	
    55	Of the eight mechanisms of `spec-to-implementation.md` §4.1, the compiled path has `nat` and `int` static parameters (the checker since climb batch 4 rung N, `3f297441c`; the run time since batch 5 rung Z, `e893a3e00`), inferring a `bool`, `dim` or `unit` one refused by name; walk has coercion since batch 4 rung C (`b628871a2`); where clauses remain the gap: a where-clause variable in an `extends` clause is undefined on both paths, and codegen refuses any declaration carrying a where clause (`CodeGen.java:2953, :4093, :5004`) (FACTS § Execution model, § The checker and the one library, § Landed semantics).
    56	
    57	The gate is strong where the 2012 team spent its last two years (codegen, the compiler front end, diagnostics) and blind where the team stopped: the bytecode optimizer (zero tests), syntax abstraction (one file), the cache round trip (not asserted), the linker, the unparser (`test-coverage.md` C.3); concurrency is seen only by the thirteen compiled `atomic` programs at four threads, since every suite runs one thread (`build.xml:947`, `:1188`).
    58	
    59	Contravariance in overloaded dispatch is switched off on every compiled program by a property that defaults true (`fortress.disable.contravariance`, `ProjectProperties.java:327-328`), the 2012 retreat of commit `c35aac139` still in force (`dormant-code.md` §2.2).
    60	
    61	The team's rationale in the specification exists only in the draft build (230 `\note{}` boxes and the Internal Document appendix, suppressed by `\ifrelease`), and its deepest layer, 27 named email threads, is not in the repository (`design-intent-sources.md` header, §4); the revival's own changes print in every build (§7, `Specification/`).
    62	
    63	## 3. Answers to the questions Pavol asked on 2026-09-16
    64	
    65	Is there a small core? The spec's own answer is no: the Internal Document's FAQ calls the core library "fictitious" and defines the language by Core versus Standard library, a split the tree does not have (`design-intent-sources.md` §4, `appendices/FAQ.tex:121-131`). What functions as the core is the mechanism layer of `spec-to-implementation.md` §4.1: traits with multiple inheritance, generics, static parameters of five kinds, operator declarations in traits, multiple dispatch, juxtaposition, coercion, where clauses. Everything numeric is library on top of that.
    66	
    67	Is the test suite shared between interpreter and compiler? No. Two hand-ported corpora: `tests/` shares no file name with `compiler_tests/`, and the 11 names it shares with `other_compiler_tests/` are different programs; only `parser_tests/` is read by both suites, and the gate's ladder stage also compiles and runs 82 files of `tests/`, each compared with its own earlier compiled output; nothing compares the two paths on one program (`test-coverage.md` B; FACTS § The harness and the gate).
    68	
    69	Where is bytecode generated? `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` (6,857 lines) writes one jar per component into `bytecode_cache` with ASM; `OverloadSet` generates dispatch methods; `NamingCzar` lowers types; generic instantiation happens later, at load time (`modules-and-phases.md` B.9, B.11).
    70	
    71	Where does the grammar extension happen? `syntax_abstractions/`, in two moments: template bodies of a grammar api are parsed when the api is analysed (GRAMMAR phase), and a component that imports the grammar gets a generated parser and is expanded by `Transform` before any phase runs on it (B.3).
    72	
    73	Is there Java interop? Yes, two mechanisms that share nothing: `builtinPrimitive("class")` in the interpreter world (368 bindings) and `import java …` in the compiler world (20 lines, `nativeHelpers/` + `nativeInterface/`); `import java` is also wired on the interpreter path by a third route, which does not work and which no test exercises (FACTS § The territory map); Java cannot call Fortress except through `MainWrapper` (B.12).
    74	
    75	Where are Fortify and Fortick, and when would we touch them? `Fortify/fortify.el` (8,024 lines) plus `fortify.sty`, driven by `bin/fortify` and an Ant task; `bin/fortick` wraps it for backtick-delimited snippets in a document; `contrib/Emacs/fortress-mode.el` is an ordinary editing mode. They are presentation only; nothing on either path depends on them (A.6, `design-intent-sources.md` §6, the notation row). The Unicode operators and juxtaposition are the language itself; Fortify only typesets them.
    76	
    77	Which spec counts? `Specification/`, "Working Draft, July 19, 2012", revision 4267. The sources under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are byte for byte the team's Working Draft of February 2011, the text `Specification/` held until the revival's revisions, and only the PDF beside them is the 1.0 artefact (FACTS "`Specification-1.0-frozen/` is byte for byte the working draft of 2011-02-02"; `spec-to-implementation.md` §1.2). This corrects the FACTS entry that called the frozen tree "1.0".
    78	
    79	## 4. Decisions the surveys put on the table
    80	
    81	Every open decision, the surveys' among them, is held in `coordinator/PLAN.md`, in the order it needs deciding ("Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed") or parked ("Off the path, parked"), and each survey's own "Decisions not made" section keeps its original list.
    82	
    83	## 5. The gaps on the path, in dependency order
    84	
    85	The path in order is `coordinator/PLAN.md`: its six phases run from the climb batches through the checker at a true zero and the switch-over to microGPT compiled and then fast, and its last section says what that order replaced, this section among it.
    86	
    87	## 6. The development loop
    88	
    89	Measured (`test-coverage.md` D): `ant compileAll` about 80 s and it wipes the interpreter cache through `cleanCache`; `ant testFast` 5 min 23 s with the wall set by the indivisible `othercompiler` track; `ant testSystem` about 2 min in four shards; `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=X` 1 min 26 s for a one-second test, the cost being ant's fileset scan of `build/`; the 280 child JVMs of the `run` tests, at about 200 ms each, are not removable; every grammar-importing run leaves a 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory (`RatsUtil.java:138-144`), swept by `experiment/env.sh`.
    90	
    91	The two suites are therefore about nine minutes after a rebuild, before the gate's other stages, and neither test target compiles, so a stale `build/` silently tests the previous revision.
    92	
    93	Three loops, fastest first, are what the path needs.
    94	
    95	The shadow loop: compile one edited file with scalac or javac against the build classpath and put it first on the classpath; seconds instead of 80 s, no rebuild, no cache wipe, no tracked change. The template prototype ran its whole matrix this way; the recipe is in `perf-probes/template-check/run-all.sh` and `matrix.sh`. This is the loop for checker and code-generator edits.
    96	
    97	The program loop: a differential check that runs the three kernels and C4 on both paths and compares output, from `explorations/`; minutes. It is not built, since nothing microGPT-shaped compiles before the switch-over; it is the loop for phases 5 and 6 of `coordinator/PLAN.md`, and the only check that would say whether the target program still works.
    98	
    99	The gate loop: the gate of §0, run once on a batch's merged tree before any commit under the sealed tree lands on `main` (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md`). Running one JUnit class directly with `junit.textui.TestRunner` and the `fastTrack` macro's properties avoids the 86 s ant tax (the template worker's recipe, `perf-probes/template-check/`).
   100	
   101	Costs worth removing, in order of payoff: split the `othercompiler` track (the only structural gain left in `testFast`); decouple `compileAll` from `cleanCache` so a rebuild does not cold-start the next interpreter run; delete the Rats! temp directory at source (`RatsUtil`, already on the worklist as a one-liner); a direct-JUnit target in `build.xml` that skips the fileset scan. All four are `build.xml` or one-file edits, gated by the suite itself.
   102	
   103	Not a loop cost but a trap: the api cache key is the source directory path and staleness is by file date (`modules-and-phases.md` B.10), so a moved tree or a same-date edit gives a silent stale result; the shadow technique sidesteps it, editing under the sealed tree does not.
   104	
   105	## 7. Touch this, and that moves
   106	
   107	Read as: change here → which path sees it → which tests guard it → where the gate is blind.
   108	
   109	| Change | Paths | Guarded by | Blind |
   110	|---|---|---|---|
   111	| `useful/` (persistent trees, `Path`, `Debug`) | both, and every module (17 importers, 1,072 imports from `nodes` alone) | 100 direct unit tests, then everything | — |
   112	| `astgen/Fortress.ast` (the AST) | both; regenerates 354,550 lines of `nodes/`, `FortressAst.scala`, `Library/FortressAst.fss`; changes the `.tfi` cache format | everything, by consequence | the cache round trip is not asserted; the generator's output is compared by mtime only |
   113	| `parser/*.rats` | both; the same rule must change in the main grammar and in `templateparser/` (the full grammar again plus `Gaps.rats`); regenerates checked-in parsers | `ParserJUTest` 188, then everything | the template parser's copy has one green program |
   114	| `parser_util/precedence_resolver/` (juxtaposition, precedence) | both, before the AST exists | 25 direct, then everything | — |
   115	| `compiler/` phases 1-4 (desugarers, disambiguator, `OverloadRewriter`) | both; which desugarers run is a `Shell` switch set per command, not the phase list (`Shell.java:268-286`, `:371-386`) | the compiler track 768 (`compiler_tests` with `parser_tests`); `testSystem` 408 for the interpreter | a desugaring gated on `use_scala`, or the compiler world's `extends Object` bound, changes one path only |
   116	| `scala_src/typechecker/` (`STypeChecker`, `STypesUtil`, `KindEnv`) | compiler only in effect; `IndexBuilder` runs on both and refuses type aliases, `test`, `property` on both; an edit to `compiler/StaticChecker.java` stales its copy in `coordinator/tools/checker-count/`, which turns the gate red | 106 `typecheck` units + every `compile`, 41 `Nat*` files among them; 22 unit tests for 59 files; the checker count | `bool`, `dim` and `unit` parameters; template ASTs (row 291); the checker count stops at the `FortressLibrary` api's first errors and never checks its component (`PLAN.md`, phase 3) |
   117	| `nodes_util/ASTIO`, `NodeReflection`, `Unprinter` (the cache serializer) | both; every api and component passes through it | 13 primitive tests | the whole-file round trip is commented out (`ASTJUTest.java:654`) |
   118	| `repository/` (`GraphRepository`, `ProjectProperties`, `ForeignJava`) and `compiler/WellKnownNames` (the world switch) | both | every suite, by consequence | the linker's aliasing (no test; an api whose component has another name links on neither path, FACTS "An exported function fails exactly as an exported variable does"); the cache key and staleness rules |
   119	| `compiler/codegen/`, `OverloadSet`, `NamingCzar` | compiler | the compiler track 768, `other_compiler_tests` 263, `library_tests` 83; 280 programs run; the ladder's 85 files | the optimizer (zero tests); where clauses and contracts refused, so never generated |
   120	| `runtimeSystem/` (`InstantiatingClassloader`, `Naming`, `BaseTask`, transactions) | compiled programs at run time; `ByteCodeWriter` and `SimpleClassLoader` also from the interpreter's `ClosureMaker` | 18 direct (naming), 280 executed programs, 119 with generics; the thirteen `atomic` programs and `FirstLoadThreadsRungG` at four threads, the last guarding the loader's first-load race (row 417, fixed by climb batch 6.5 rung G) | concurrency beyond those fourteen; transactions (one JUnit assertion) |
   121	| `interpreter/` (evaluator, values, types, its own tasks and transactions) | interpreter | `testSystem` 408 (pass = no exception and no `fail` in output) | a wrong number the program does not check itself; concurrency (`FORTRESS_THREADS=1` per shard) |
   122	| `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and the other interpreter-world `.fss` | interpreter; the compiled checker, in the checker count; the compiled path from the switch-over; the specification's Part IV, generated from its `.fsi` (`Specification/library/default-libraries.tex:27,39`) | `testSystem` 408; the checker count; `SpecData` 133 and `demos` 62 outside the gate | the compiled path does not link it before the switch-over |
   123	| `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`, `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`, `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` | compiler, every compiled program, until the switch-over deletes them; nothing is added to them (POSITIONS 2026-09-21) | `library_tests` 83 directly; 280 programs by consequence | `RR64` in 12 executed programs, `NN32` in 7, `NN64` in 5 |
   124	| `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss` | both | everything | — |
   125	| `nativeHelpers/`, `compiler/nativeInterface/` | compiler (`import java`); the wrapper generator wraps every method of a named class, private ones too, and fails the import on an unmappable type (FACTS "Two constraints of the test and native machinery") | 25 executed programs import one, no direct test | the interpreter's `import java` route does not work and has no test (FACTS § The territory map) |
   126	| `syntax_abstractions/` | both, before phase 1 | 19 unit tests, one green program | 16 of 17 whole-program tests red as shipped, not re-checked since; nothing on the compile path |
   127	| `Shell.java` flags and phase orders | both; which desugarings and which checks run per path | every CommandTest and every `run` subprocess | `typecheck-old` fails by design |
   128	| `build.xml`, `default_repository/configuration` | the suites and the source path; `fortress.unittests.noopt` hides 283 tests; `compileAll` deletes the tracked `default_repository/caches/global.map` (FACTS "`ant compileAll` deletes a tracked file") | the suite, by running it | a stale `build/` is tested silently |
   129	| `bin/fortress`, `bin/run`, `bin/run_classpath` | the two JVMs and their classpaths; `JAVA_FLAGS`, whose absence gives `bin/fortress` a 256 MB heap, not the harness's 768 MB (FACTS "Three heaps run the interpreter") | `shelltests` (2, reachable only by hand) | — |
   130	| `Specification/` (the standard) | neither path; the PDF (`./ant genSource`, `./ant tex` in `Specification/fortress/`); each change a `\revision` callout plus an Appendix I entry quoting the original (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, S1) | the build | the text against the library, except at a gather whose brief asks (POSITIONS 2026-09-26, the number chapters) |
   131	| `explorations/apl/mg/`, `run-c4/src/` (the target program) | interpreter; compiled, its eighteen components stop at name resolution until the switch-over | the 40 checks, by hand, never in the gate (POSITIONS 2026-09-19); the ladder holds the eighteen at their phase | no four-thread run since rung F changed two model lines (`run-c4/cold-cache/ROWS.md`; `compile-ladder/rung-flat-tower/REPORT.md` § 10) |
   132	
   133	Two cycles to keep in mind when ordering edits: `compiler ↔ scala_src` (200/111 imports) and `compiler ↔ interpreter` (18/28; `Driver` and `WellKnownNames` need each other), so a change in the checker's Java index layer is a change on both paths (`modules-and-phases.md` A.3).
   134	
   135	## 8. What this map does not settle
   136	
   137	Every open decision, which `coordinator/PLAN.md` holds in the order it needs deciding. Those are Pavol's.

1	# Repo internals: how to move around this codebase
     2	
     3	Living notes on the architecture and the techniques that proved useful while
     4	working on the revival. Started 2026-08-19; extend as new things are learned.
     5	Companion documents: `test-baseline-jdk8.md` (test-suite state, compiler-path
     6	discovery narrative), root `CLAUDE.md` (build recipe, quick facts).
     7	
     8	## Module map (verified 2026-08-21)
     9	
    10	Every count below was measured against the working tree at HEAD; this
    11	replaces folklore from the old READMEs.
    12	
    13	### Top level
    14	
    15	Live toolchain: `ProjectFortress/` (293 MB — all Java/Scala source, test
    16	corpora, third-party jars), root `build.xml`, `bin/` (35 scripts),
    17	`SpecData/` (133 spec-extracted `.fss` examples, run by `ant testSpecData`),
    18	`Fortify/` (Emacs-batch LaTeX renderer — `fortify.el` + `fortify.sty` typeset
    19	Fortress source as math for the spec/papers, via `bin/fortify` and
    20	`ant_tasks/FortifyTask`), `contrib/` (Atom/Emacs/GtkSourceView/Vim modes).
    21	Note: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is an 18-line deprecation stub — the root
    22	`build.xml` (1,633 lines, 68 targets) is the only real build file.
    23	
    24	Standard library: `Library/` (53 `.fss`/`.fsi` pairs; `FortressLibrary.fss`
    25	is the 4,518-line prelude), top-level `CompilerLibrary/` (10 `.fsi`-only API
    26	stubs for the compiler path — easy to confuse with `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`),
    27	and — surprisingly — `lib/` (Fortress source: `List`, `Queue`, `Test`; not
    28	jars — those live in `ProjectFortress/third_party/`).
    29	
    30	Spec and papers: `Specification/` (365 MB — 55% of the repo, mostly LaTeX
    31	build residue), `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, `Papers/`, `Documentation/`.
    32	
    33	Revival era: `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`.
    34	
    35	Historical artifacts / dead weight: `BasicCoreFortress/` (core-calculus
    36	experiment), `Sandbox/`, `CommunityMetrics/` (SVN-era metrics scripts),
    37	`NeedBetterErrorMessages/` (single-file TODO bucket), `DOT_idea/` +
    38	`PFC_DOT_iml` + `ECLIPSE/` (Sun-era IDE configs).
    39	
    40	### Packages under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`
    41	
    42	22 packages plus the loose `Shell.java` (1,288 lines) — the CLI dispatcher
    43	(`compile`, `run`, `walk`, `link`, `api`, `parse`, `unparse`, `typecheck`,
    44	`test`, `junit`, … parsed at Shell.java:403–487).
    45	
    46	| Package | Files | Role |
    47	|---|---|---|
    48	| `nodes/` | 1,071 java | ASTGen-generated AST classes + visitors (committed, regenerable) |
    49	| `interpreter/` | 246 java | Tree-walking evaluator: `evaluator/` 169, `glue/` 53 (native prims), `env/` 15, `rewrite/` 7 |
    50	| `compiler/` | 197 java + 10 scala | Static phases + JVM backend: `asmbytecodeoptimizer/` 43, `index/` 34, `runtimeValues/` 30, `codegen/` 15, `phases/` 14, `disambiguator/` 13, `desugarer/` 16 (7 scala); top level holds `Disambiguator`, `Desugarer`, `NamingCzar`, `OverloadSet`, `WellKnownNames`, `GlobalEnvironment` |
    51	| `useful/` | 131 java | Utility layer dominated by hand-rolled persistent balanced-tree collections (`BATree`, `BASet`, `BATreeEC`), tests interleaved |
    52	| `parser_util/` | 89 java | Hand-written parser support: precedence/juxtaposition resolution, layout, grammar-coverage instrumentation |
    53	| `parser/` | 5 java + 62 other | Rats!/xtc packrat parsers — **four grammars** (61 `.rats`): main `Fortress.rats`, `preparser/` (import/grammar discovery), `templateparser/` (syntax-abstraction templates), `import_collector/`. Four generated parsers are huge (`Fortress.java` 2.06 MB, `TemplateParser.java` 2.16 MB); committed, regenerable |
    54	| `scala_src/` | 59 scala | **The real type checker**: `typechecker/` 27 (+ `impls`, `staticenv`), `useful/` 15, `types/` 7, `linker/` 4, `overloading/` 3, `disambiguator/` 2, `nodes/` 1 (generated). Started Feb 2009 as a Scala rewrite of the Java checker (whose stubs remain in `compiler/typechecker/`) |
    55	| `syntax_abstractions/` | 30 java | Extensible syntax: user-defined grammars generate new parsers at compile time |
    56	| `nodes_util/` | 29 java + 1 scala | Hand-written AST factories/utilities: `NodeFactory`, `ExprFactory`, `NodeUtil`, `Span`, `ASTIO` |
    57	| `exceptions/` | 26 java + 1 scala | Error hierarchy: `StaticError`, `ProgramError`, `TypeError`, `CompilerBug`, `InterpreterBug`, … |
    58	| `runtimeSystem/` | 25 java | Work-stealing runtime + `Naming`/`Instantiater` (generic instantiation at class-load time) that emitted bytecode links against |
    59	| `nativeHelpers/` | 24 java | FFI shims for `import java` library functions (compiler world) |
    60	| `astgen/` | 16 java | Fortress extensions to Rice's ASTGen: visitor generators, `FortressAstGenerator`, `ScalaAstGenerator` |
    61	| `repository/` | 16 java | Component cache/graph: `CacheBasedRepository`, `GraphRepository`, `ForeignJava`, and `ProjectProperties` — the `FORTRESS_HOME`/`BASEDIR`/cache-path resolver everything routes through; first stop when paths misbehave |
    62	| `tests/` | 16 java | `tests/unit_tests/` — the JUnit harnesses (`SystemJUTest`, `CompilerJUTest`, `OtherCompilerJUTest`, `FileTests`) driving the `.fss` corpora |
    63	| `numerics/` | 6 java | BLAS JNI binding, directed-rounding IEEE support |
    64	| `ant_tasks/` | 6 java | Ant tasks: `fortress`, `fortify`, `fortex`, `foreg`, `fortick` |
    65	| `linker/` | 5 java | Component linking / api-to-implementation binding |
    66	| `unicode/` | 4 java | Generates operator/precedence tables from Unicode data files |
    67	| `tools/` | 2 java | `FortressAstToConcrete` — AST→source unparser behind `fortress unparse`; handy for debugging desugaring |
    68	| `fib_tests/`, `unit_tests/` | 1 each | Stray: a benchmark harness; one near-empty Scala JUnit |
    69	
    70	### Test corpora (`.fss` under `ProjectFortress/`)
    71	
    72	`tests/` 381 (interpreter, → `testSystem`), `compiler_tests/` 456 + 35 `.fsi`,
    73	`other_compiler_tests/` 178, `parser_tests/` 112, `demos/` 62,
    74	`syntax_abstraction_tests/` 43, `library_tests/` 26, `linker_tests/` 9,
    75	`compiler_regressions/` 6. Known-failing corpora are parked in sibling dirs
    76	(`not_passing_yet/` 58, `not_working_*`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`,
    77	`long_term_not_working/`). There is **no `static_tests/`** — the class
    78	`compiler/StaticTestSuite.java` does not correspond to a directory.
    79	
    80	### One edit, many files
    81	
    82	`ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` (2,125 lines; a sibling of `src/`, not
    83	the `astgen` Java package) regenerates `nodes/` (all 1,071 files),
    84	`scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, and `Library/FortressAst.fss`/`.fsi`
    85	via `ant makeAST` — all four outputs are committed, so a stale `.ast` edit
    86	silently diverges from the checked-in tree (see "Generated code" below).
    87	
    88	### Git-history caveat for this map
    89	
    90	`git log -- <dir>` is unusable for dating anything: the Mercurial-to-git
    91	conversion behind `sirinath/fortress`, of which this repository is a fork,
    92	cut 146 parent links, leaving parentless full-tree snapshot roots at which
    93	path-limited history from HEAD dead-ends instead of reaching 2007 (see
    94	`explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`). Use `git log --follow` on individual files
    95	(that is how the Feb 2009 start of the Scala type checker was confirmed).
    96	
    97	## The two worlds
    98	
    99	The tree contains two nearly-disjoint executions of Fortress, and most
   100	confusion comes from mixing them up:
   101	
   102	| | interpreter ("walk") | bytecode compiler |
   103	|---|---|---|
   104	| era | 2003-lineage, mature | 2010–2012, the team's final push, incomplete |
   105	| entry | `fortress <file>.fss` | `fortress compile <file>.fss` + `fortress run <component>` |
   106	| libraries | `Library/` + `LibraryBuiltin/` (FortressBuiltin, NativeArray, ...) | `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra`, `CompilerSystem`, `GeneratorLibrary` |
   107	| native mechanism | `builtinPrimitive("com.sun...glue.prim.X")` in .fss | `import java com.sun...nativeHelpers.{...}` in .fss |
   108	| native String type | glue-level FString | `CompilerBuiltin.JavaString` / `StringVector` (foreign map in `NamingCzar`) |
   109	| tests | `ProjectFortress/tests/` via `ant testSystem` | `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` via `ant testFast` etc. |
   110	
   111	The mode switch is `com.sun.fortress.compiler.WellKnownNames`:
   112	`useInterpreterLibraries()` / `useCompilerLibraries()` swap the meaning of
   113	"the builtin library" (`FortressBuiltin` vs `CompilerBuiltin`) and "the
   114	standard library" (`FortressLibrary` vs `CompilerLibrary`). `Shell.subMain`
   115	calls one or the other per subcommand (`walk` vs `compile`/`run`/`link`).
   116	
   117	Consequences:
   118	- A `.fss` file is generally written for ONE world. `import java ...` means
   119	  compiler-only; `builtinPrimitive` means interpreter-only.
   120	- An *api name* used by both worlds is trouble: apis resolve by name along a
   121	  single shared source path (see below). This is exactly what broke the six
   122	  interpreter tests in the 2012 endgame (`api System` shadowed — see
   123	  test-baseline postscript) and why the compiler apis are `Compiler*`-prefixed.
   124	
   125	## The pipeline, phase by phase (verified 2026-09-08 from `compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java` and `Shell.java`)
   126	
   127	Both execution paths share one phase list and differ only at the end. Parse (`parser/`, Rats!) produces the AST (`nodes/`); then PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE (names bound to declarations), GRAMMAR (syntax extensions), PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, TYPECHECK (`scala_src/typechecker/`, writes a static type on every expression; no new representation), DESUGAR (comprehensions and big operators to `generate` calls with reduction objects, coercions, chained comparisons, getters/setters), then OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN on the compiler path (`compilerPhaseOrder`, which also has INTEGERLITERALFOLDING before TYPECHECK) or OVERLOADREWRITE_FOR_INTERPRETER on the interpreter path (`interpreterPhaseOrder`). The AST is the only intermediate representation from parse to bytecode; there is no lower IR and no optimizing middle.
   128	
   129	The TYPECHECK phase is in the interpreter's list but is a no-op there: `walk` calls `setScala(false)` and the checking flag `fortress.compile.typecheck` defaults to false, and `StaticChecker` returns the tree untouched when off. `compile`/`build` set it on. Consequently the interpreter runs untyped desugared trees and accepts spec-illegal programs (e.g. `Value extends Number` against `Number comprises {RR64}`), and there is no command-line switch to enable checking for `walk`.
   130	
   131	What the code generator does with the static types: every Fortress type is lowered to a JVM reference type (traits to interfaces, objects to classes, `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64` via `NamingCzar`; `CodeGen.java` emits no `DADD`), every overloaded name gets one generated dispatch method that tests argument types from most to least specific (symmetric multimethod dispatch on run-time types), and generic declarations are compiled once as templates whose instantiations (`Box⟦RR64⟧`, oxford brackets from `Naming.java`) are stamped out by `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java` at first use by ASM rewriting of the template bytes; instantiation renames, it does not change representation. Emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6 because the load-time rewriting pipeline does not maintain stack-map frames and the JVM verifier may fall back to type inference only at that version. The `value` modifier on objects (spec: immutable fields, no identity) has no representation meaning in codegen.
   132	
   133	## Name resolution: fortress.source.path
   134	
   135	`default_repository/configuration` (overridable via `local_repository/`,
   136	`~/.fortress/`, `./.fortress/`, env vars, or `-D` flags) defines:
   137	
   138	    fortress.source.path=;.;${_fr}/LibraryBuiltin;${FORTRESS_AUTOHOME}/Library;${_fr}/test_library
   139	
   140	- Leading `;` sets the separator (Windows compat). `.` (cwd!) is searched
   141	  FIRST, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, then `Library/`.
   142	- `import Foo` finds the first `Foo.fsi`/`Foo.fss` on that path. First hit
   143	  wins — a file earlier on the path silently shadows a later one, and cwd can
   144	  shadow everything (mind where you run from).
   145	- The interpreter requires filename (sans suffix) == component/api name.
   146	
   147	## Cache anatomy and hygiene
   148	
   149	`default_repository/caches/` (gitignored by path, as is
   150	`ProjectFortress/test-caches/`; a cache written anywhere else, such as a
   151	probe's own `-Dfortress.caches` directory, is not ignored):
   152	- `analyzed_cache/`, `*parsed_cache/` — front-end analysis, shared-ish
   153	  between worlds; the main source of cross-world contamination.
   154	- `interpreter_cache/`, `environment_cache/` — interpreter side.
   155	- `bytecode_cache/` — compiler output: one jar per compiled component;
   156	  library components get api-qualified names (`fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`).
   157	- `nativewrapper_cache/` — generated wrappers for `import java` natives.
   158	
   159	Rules learned the hard way:
   160	- **Recompile what you edited; a wipe is not the fix.** Stale or order-inconsistent
   161	  caches produce *misleading* runtime errors
   162	  (`NoSuchMethodError: CompilerBuiltin.println(...)`,
   163	  `NoSuchMethodError: ...asJavaString()`, `Unable to read serialized data
   164	  ... recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink`). These
   165	  are cache problems, not compiler bugs: recompile the component in the
   166	  library order (below), and run the library order after `ant compileAll`.
   167	- After editing a compiler-library `.fss` (`CompilerBuiltin`,
   168	  `CompilerLibrary` and the rest), `fortress compile` that component; the
   169	  interpreter's library (`FortressLibrary.fss` and the rest) needs nothing,
   170	  since walk re-reads it on its next run. What to recompile after each kind
   171	  of edit is the `fortress-repo` skill's `build-and-caches.md`.
   172	- **Compile order matters** on a fresh cache, because `fortress compile` of a
   173	  program does NOT emit the builtin-library jars, and the runtime classloader
   174	  then falls back to the **bootstrap stubs** in `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`
   175	  (ant-compiled from checked-in `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/*.java` —
   176	  a *frozen, older* snapshot of CompilerBuiltin!). Symptom: NoSuchMethodError
   177	  on a method that plainly exists in CompilerBuiltin.fss. Recipe:
   178	
   179	      cd ProjectFortress
   180	      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss
   181	      ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss
   182	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss
   183	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss
   184	      ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss
   185	      ../bin/fortress compile <program>.fss
   186	      ../bin/fortress run <component> [args...]
   187	
   188	  The JUnit harness gets this right because `CompilerJUTest` starts with
   189	  `Shell.resetRepository()` and compiles the world in dependency order.
   190	
   191	## Toolchain traps (JDK rungs)
   192	
   193	- **build.xml's javac tasks originally set `source=` but never `target=`**
   194	  (and three set neither). Harmless on JDK 8 (target defaulted to 8); on
   195	  JDK 11 target defaulted to 11 → v55 classfiles with invokedynamic string
   196	  concat → ASM 3.1's ClassReader (used by `ForeignJava.findClass` for every
   197	  `import java ...`) dies with `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`, failing all
   198	  compiler-path tests while testSystem stays green. Fixed by pinning
   199	  `target="${javaSourceVersion}"` on all 8 javac tasks (commit fdd4a57c2).
   200	  Diagnosis trick: a 20-line probe compiling against
   201	  `third_party/asm/asm-all-3.1.jar` + `javap -v | grep major` pinpoints
   202	  exactly which classfile ASM chokes on. (Surprise: JDK 11's *platform*
   203	  classes parse fine under `SKIP_DEBUG|SKIP_FRAMES|SKIP_CODE`; it was our
   204	  own freshly compiled v55 output that broke.)
   205	- `default_repository/caches/global.map`, the linker's state at the caches
   206	  root, is untracked and gitignored like the rest of the caches: the linker
   207	  writes an empty map wherever it is missing
   208	  (`linker/RepoState.java:366-385`), so `ant compileAll` or a wipe of
   209	  `default_repository/caches/*` needs no restore.
   210	
   211	## Generated code
   212	
   213	- Churn in the generated sources after a build is a regression to investigate,
   214	  never noise to revert.
   215	- AST nodes (`src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/`, 1000+ files),
   216	  `scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, `Library/FortressAst.fsi/fss` are all
   217	  generated by astgen from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` (build
   218	  target `makeAST`). They are checked in; ant's uptodate check compares
   219	  mtimes, so a fresh checkout looks current. If scalac errors show arity
   220	  mismatches in `S*Pattern` nodes: `touch ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast
   221	  && ant compileAll`.
   222	- Parser (`parser/*.java` from Rats! grammars), `precedence_resolver/
   223	  Operators.java` (from unicode data) — same pattern.
   224	
   225	## Test harness mechanics
   226	
   227	- Targets: `testFast` (unit + compiler suites, ~12 min, excludes interpreter
   228	  system tests), `testSystem` (interpreter, 382 tests, ~2 min),
   229	  `testLibrary`, `testCompiler`, `testNotPassing` (expected failures),
   230	  `testDemos`, nightly variants. Plain-text results land in
   231	  `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/TEST-<class>.txt`.
   232	- `.test` files (in `compiler_tests/` etc.) are property files driving
   233	  `FileTests`: keys like `compile`, `run`, `tests=`, `compile_err_equals=`
   234	  decide which phases run and what output to expect. `run`-tests execute the
   235	  compiled program via the `bin/run` script in a subprocess.
   236	- To reproduce one interpreter test: `../bin/fortress tests/<Name>.fss`
   237	  (from `ProjectFortress/`). Failures print the real diagnostic that the
   238	  JUnit boilerplate hides.
   239	- Suite runs reset/repopulate `default_repository/caches` — don't interleave
   240	  ad-hoc compiles with a running suite, and don't trust cache state after one.
   241	
   242	## Git archaeology techniques
   243	
   244	- **The history has a parallel root**: `5a68404` (David Chase, 2012-07-19,
   245	  4372 files) is a parentless import later merged by `575fe64`. Any
   246	  `git log <base>..HEAD -- <file>` therefore lists `5a68404` for almost
   247	  every file — useless for "who changed what since June". Use **content
   248	  comparison** instead: `git diff --quiet <base> HEAD -- <file>` and
   249	  `git show <base>:<file> | cmp - <other-tree>/<file>`.
   250	- The twelve pre-2016 branches are hg named-branch relics; the 2008 research
   251	  branches were squash-merged into trunk, so fine-grained authorship exists
   252	  only on the branch heads. Full survey with per-branch verdicts: see the
   253	  session notes / ask before deleting anything.
   254	- hg conversion quirks: empty "Starting/Closing branch X" marker commits;
   255	  `.hgignore` still in tree; David Chase's 2012-01-20 branch-closing sweep.
   256	
   257	## Environment gotchas (cloud container)
   258	
   259	- Current rung JDK 25 (`/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64`; 8/11/17/21 also
   260	  gated green); `unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` or the proxy's trust-store flags
   261	  pollute every JVM fork.
   262	- `web.archive.org` and `labs.oracle.com` are blocked by network policy —
   263	  research PDFs must be uploaded into the session by Pavol. Archived *pages*
   264	  (not PDFs) can be read via the pure.md relay; see the method note in
   265	  `research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md`.
   266	- Gitignored files (e.g. `research/decks/*.pdf`) do not survive the
   267	  container; only commits and pushes persist.
