47	
48	## B.2 Rats! parsing
49	
50	There are four grammars, and the build generates four parsers from them with the Rats! generator inside `third_party/xtc/xtc.jar`.
51	
52	`build.xml` invokes `xtc.parser.Rats` as a forked Java process, once per grammar, through the `buildparser` macro (`build.xml:1400-1424`); the targets are `fortressparser`, `preparser`, `importcollector`, `templateparser` (`build.xml:1427-1450`), all four driven by `parser` (`build.xml:1480-1487`), which `compileAll` depends on.
53	
54	The generated `.java` files are checked in, and the up-to-date test is mtime-based over the `.rats` sources (`build.xml:1331-1351`), so a fresh checkout looks current — the same trap as the AST nodes.
55	
56	The macro rewrites the generation date out of the generated header afterwards so regeneration is byte-identical (`build.xml:1416-1423`); that normalization is revival-era.
57	
58	At run time the four parsers are used as follows.
59	
60	`ImportCollector` runs first on every component, returning a compilation unit that contains only the imports, so the system can see which grammars a component imports before it can parse it (`compiler/Parser.java:156-176`, called from `macroParse` at `:114`).
61	
62	`PreFortress` runs on every file whose parse is about to be attempted, purely to produce readable syntax errors: its errors are collected from a log file and reported instead of the packrat parser's (`compiler/Parser.java:415-428`, used at `:323-327`).
63	
64	`Fortress` is the real parser; after it succeeds, `parser_util/SyntaxChecker` walks the tree for the rules the grammar cannot express (`compiler/Parser.java:346-366`).
65	
66	`TemplateParser` is never used directly; it is the base that every generated user-grammar parser extends (B.3).
67	
68	The grammars call into `parser_util/` for everything context-sensitive: juxtaposition and operator precedence are resolved by `precedence_resolver/` from the table in `Operators.java`, which `ant operatorsGen` generates from Unicode data (`build.xml:387-391`).
69	
70	## B.3 Grammar extension expansion
71	
72	A user grammar is compiled in two places, at two different times, and the distinction matters.
73	
74	First, when the **api** that declares the grammar is analysed, the GRAMMAR phase runs `GrammarRewriter.rewriteApis` (`phases/GrammarPhase.java:40`), which does six rewrites on the grammar declarations (item disambiguation, whitespace elimination, escape rewriting, extension desugaring, transformer naming; `GrammarRewriter.java:72-107`) and then parses the templates (`:116-125`).
75	
76	Parsing a template means: generate a parser for *this grammar* (`TemplateParser.java:97` → `ParserMaker.parserForGrammar`, `ParserMaker.java:79`), then run the template body text through it at the nonterminal the rule declares, by reflection on the Rats! method name (`TemplateParser.java:101-125,160-166`).
77	
78	The result is an ordinary AST fragment containing `TemplateGap` nodes where the rule's variables appear; that fragment replaces the unparsed transformer text (`TemplateParser.java:50-58`). This is the moment a template body stops being a string.
79	
80	Second, when a **component** that imports such a grammar is read, `Parser.macroParse` notices the imported grammars (`compiler/Parser.java:111-135`, `getImportedGrammars` at `:212`), composes them into a PEG and generates a parser for the component (`parseWithGrammars`, `:259-275`).
81	
82	That generation is a full Rats! run plus a `javac` run, at program-compile time, in a fresh temporary directory: `RatsParserGenerator.generateParser` clones the base and template grammars into `/tmp/fortress…rats` (`RatsUtil.getTempDir`, `RatsUtil.java:138-146`), calls `xtc.parser.Rats.main` (`RatsParserGenerator.java:53`), compiles the emitted parser with `com.sun.tools.javac.Main.compile` (`rats/JavaC.java:39`), and loads it with a one-off class loader (`RatsParserGenerator.java:61-66`).
83	
84	The temporary directory is never deleted; that is the disk-filling behaviour already on record in FACTS ("The container").
85	
86	The component is then parsed with that generated parser, and the resulting tree — which contains `_SyntaxTransformation` nodes where user syntax was used — is expanded by `Transform.transform` (`compiler/Parser.java:281`, `syntax_abstractions/phases/Transform.java:61`).
87	
88	`Transform` is the macro expander: for each `_SyntaxTransformation` it looks up the named transformer from the api (`Transform.java:72-83`), evaluates its argument nodes, and runs the transformer's template through `TransformerEvaluator` (`:613-679,706`); a `TemplateGap` is replaced by the bound value (`:541-555`); hygiene renames binders written literally in a template (`:110-117`).
89	
90	Where this sits in the pipeline: expansion happens **before** any phase runs on the component, because `GraphRepository.refreshGraph` calls `syntaxExpand(node)` and passes its result into `parseComponent` (`GraphRepository.java:511`), and `parseComponent` is what calls `Shell.analyze` (`:805`). So the GRAMMAR phase position in the phase array applies to apis only; a program's user syntax is already gone by phase 1.
91	
92	This machinery is on both paths: `syntaxExpand` is in the shared repository, GRAMMAR is in `compilerPhaseOrder` (`phases/PhaseOrder.java:140`), and the only thing that stops a grammar-importing program from compiling is the prelude collision recorded in FACTS ("A user grammar on the compile path").
93	
94	`Shell.withMacro()` (`Shell.java:244`, property `fortress.compile.macro`, default true at `:1274`) is the switch that bypasses the whole mechanism.
95	
96	## B.4 Disambiguation
97	
98	`Disambiguator.disambiguateApis`/`disambiguateComponents` (`compiler/Disambiguator.java:121,257`) run, in order, `SelfParamDisambiguator`, `TypeDisambiguator`, `NonterminalDisambiguator` (apis only) and `ExprDisambiguator` (`:90,145,153,185,300,308,362`).
99	
100	`ExprDisambiguator` is Scala (`scala_src/disambiguator/ExprDisambiguator.scala`, 1,102 lines with its sibling) and it is where a bare name becomes either a `VarRef` or an `FnRef` carrying every function of that name in scope (`:432-440`).
101	
102	What it writes into the `FnRef` matters for both paths: the *interpreter* candidate list is the full set of matching names, the *new* list is the unambiguous names; the type checker later narrows the second, and the interpreter uses the first (`OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`).
103	
104	Output is the same AST with names bound; nothing downstream re-resolves names, and the `.tfi`/`.tfs` cache is written after this and later phases, which is why a cache from one library world poisons the other.
105	
106	## B.5 Desugaring
107	
108	There are three desugaring phases and they are split by what has to be known, not by which path is running.
109	
110	PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR must precede name binding because it introduces calls to names (`PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.java:39-52`).
111	
112	PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR produces code that must itself be type-checked: comprehensions and big operators become `__generate`/`__bigOperator`/`__bigOperator2` calls against the library's reduction objects, generator lists become `exp.loop(fn x => body, gs)` chains, and generalized `if`/`while` become `__cond`/`__whileCond` (`PreTypeCheckDesugaringVisitor.java:142-165,245,301,333-335`).
113	
114	DESUGAR runs after type checking because getter/setter and coercion rewriting need types (`compiler/Desugarer.java:36-45`).
115	
116	Which visitors run is controlled by `Shell` flags, and this is where the two paths quietly differ: `useInterpreterLibraries` sets `compiled_expr_desugaring` false (`Shell.java:379-386`), so on `walk` the case-expression desugarer (`Desugarer.java:124-127`), the type-ascription desugarer (`:140-144`), the typecase desugarer and the abstract-marking pass (`PreTypeCheckDesugarer.java:117-126`) are all skipped, while coercion and getter/setter desugaring run on both (defaults at `Shell.java:1277,1283`).
117	
118	`Desugarer.desugarApi` is a no-op — it returns the api unchanged (`compiler/Desugarer.java:82-85`).
119	
120	After the phase chain, the interpreter runs one more rewrite of its own that the compiler has no counterpart for: `RewriteInPresenceOfTypeInfoVisitor` then `DesugarerVisitor`, which annotate every variable, function and operator reference with its lexical nesting depth (`interpreter/env/ComponentWrapper.java:109-111`, `interpreter/rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java:30,61-85`). The result is cached in `interpreter_cache` (`ComponentWrapper.java:96,112-114`).
121	
122	## B.6 Type checking
123	
124	`TypeCheckPhase` builds indexes for the apis and components, checks the apis, then the components (`phases/TypeCheckPhase.java:32-58`); the work is in `StaticChecker.checkCompilationUnit` (`compiler/StaticChecker.java:163`).
125	
126	For an api: compound-api check, api linking, type-hierarchy acyclicity, well-formedness (`:174-220`).
127	
128	For a component: `ApiTypeExtractor`, `TypeNormalizer`, a `TraitTable` and a `TypeAnalyzer`, then `Thunker` to give elided return types thunks, then `STypeChecker.typeCheck` (`:196-247`), then well-formedness again, overloading rules, export checking and the variance checker (`:268-290`).
129	
130	The checker writes a type onto each expression node and produces no new representation, which is why the same `nodes/` tree continues into DESUGAR.
131	
132	The variance checker is skipped when `compiled_expr_desugaring` is off, with the comment "Hack: don't run the variance checker if running the interpreter" (`StaticChecker.java:289-290`) — one of the few places in the checker that names the interpreter at all.
133	
134	`Shell.getScala()` selects between the Scala checker and a Java one that no longer exists (`StaticChecker.java:228-230`); `setScala(false)` is set by `walk` (`Shell.java:422`), `typecheck-old` (`:467`), `test` (`:475`), the bare-filename arm (`:481`) and the `-typecheck-java` flag (`:865`).
135	
136	## B.7 Overloading
137	
138	Resolution is split between a shared rewrite and two completely different dispatch mechanisms.
139	
140	The shared part: `OverloadRewriter` replaces a reference that has several candidates with a reference to a single synthetic name spelled `f{f1,f2,…}` and appends a `_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` declaring it (`compiler/OverloadRewriter.java:74-92`, `OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:110-142`).
141	
142	On the interpreter path, `BuildTopLevelEnvironments.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`interpreter/evaluator/BuildTopLevelEnvironments.java:128`) turns that declaration into an `OverloadedFunction`, and the actual selection happens per call, on run-time values, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatch` (`interpreter/evaluator/values/OverloadedFunction.java:787`); failure is the familiar "Failed to find any matching overload" (`:795`).
143	
144	On the compiler path, `CodeGen.for_RewriteFnOverloadDecl` (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6409`) hands the declaration to `OverloadSet`, which emits one dispatch method per overloaded name, testing argument types from most to least specific (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:1944,1964`).
145	
146	So the same phase feeds a run-time search in one world and a generated decision tree in the other, and the candidate lists they start from are different (`OverloadRewriteVisitor.java:107`): the interpreter's comes from the disambiguator, the compiler's from the type checker.
147	
148	## B.8 The interpreter tail
149	
150	`Shell.eval` asks the repository for a *linked* component (`Shell.java:620`, `GraphRepository.getLinkedComponent:883`), which is what pulls the library components — not just their apis — into the graph (`GraphRepository.java:891-902`).
151	
152	`Driver.evalComponent` (`interpreter/Driver.java:78`) then does the linking by hand: it builds a `ComponentWrapper` per component, installs the primitives into `AnyType`'s environment, forces `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin` to be present (`:140-162`), closes over the import graph, then runs `preloadTopLevel`, a fixed-point pass over trait information, and environment population.
153	
154	`Driver.runProgram` creates the ForkJoin pool (`FortressTaskRunnerGroup`, sized by `FORTRESS_THREADS`, `:521-532,556`), registers the program arguments, and invokes an `EvaluatorTask` (`:554-570`), which calls back into `Driver.runProgramTask` (`interpreter/evaluator/tasks/EvaluatorTask.java:46`) to look up the `run` closure and invoke it (`Driver.java:501-513`).
155	
156	From there it is `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator`, a `NodeAbstractVisitor` over the rewritten AST, with values from `evaluator/values/` and types from `evaluator/types/`.
157	
158	Implicit parallelism and transactions are the interpreter's own: tuple elements and operator operands become `TupleTask`s (`Evaluator.java:267`), and `atomic`/`tryatomic` enter the STM in `evaluator/transactions/` (`Evaluator.java:183,204,210`).
159	
160	## B.9 The compiler tail
161	
162	`CodeGenerationPhase` runs, per component, a `FreeVariables` pass, a `FreeVarTypes` pass and a `ParallelismAnalyzer`, then `CodeGen` (`phases/CodeGenerationPhase.java:183-196`).
163	
164	`CodeGen`'s constructor opens the output jar immediately — `NamingCzar.cache + <dotted component name> + ".jar"` in `bytecode_cache` (`codegen/CodeGen.java:391-393`, `compiler/NamingCzar.java:132`) — which is why a failed compile leaves a truncated jar behind.
165	
166	Classes are written with ASM `COMPUTE_FRAMES` through `CodeGenClassWriter`/`ManglingClassWriter` (`CodeGen.java:406`); generic declarations are emitted once as templates, to be stamped out at load time (B.11).
167	
168	For apis that were synthesized from `import java`, the same phase asks `ForeignJava` to generate wrappers (`CodeGenerationPhase.java:94`, `repository/ForeignJava.java:757,807` → `compiler/nativeInterface/FortressTransformer.java:37`), which writes them into `nativewrapper_cache` (`FortressTransformer.java:33`).
169	
170	There is no link step that produces a single artifact: `fortress compile` leaves jars, and `fortress run` finds them by classpath.
171	
172	`fortress link` and `fortress build` differ from `compile` only in passing `doLink=true` (`Shell.java:1063`), which makes the repository add the library *components* to the graph (`GraphRepository.java:883-902`) — that is, in principle, the single command that compiles the world in the right order, as opposed to the hand-ordered recipe in `repo-internals.md:170-180`.
173	
174	## B.10 The repository, the cache, and `.tfi`/`.tfs`
175	
176	`GraphRepository` is the compilation manager for both paths: it builds a graph of api and component nodes over the source path, decides what is stale, and drives parsing and analysis in dependency order (`repository/GraphRepository.java:479-524`).
177	
178	Apis are parsed all at once (`:713-745`); components must be done one at a time and in order, because syntax expansion may need other components to have been parsed already (`:503-512`).
179	
180	The default library is seeded as graph roots from `WellKnownNames.defaultLibrary()` (`GraphRepository.java:125-128,133-165`), which is the single switch between the two worlds: `useFortressLibraries` makes it `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin`, `AnyType`; `useCompilerLibraries` makes it `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `AnyType` (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:113-137`).
181	
182	Analysis results are serialized as text: `ASTIO.writeJavaAst` writes a parenthesized dump of the node tree (`nodes_util/ASTIO.java:92-120`) and `FortressNodeReader`/`Unprinter`/`interpreter/reader/Lex` read it back (`ASTIO.java:142-160`).
183	
184	The file name is the api name plus a hex hash — and the hash is of the **source directory path**, not of the content (`compiler/NamingCzar.java:244-254`): `AnyType-6d4f5273.tfi`. Two files of the same api name on different path entries therefore get different cache files, and moving the tree invalidates everything.
185	
186	`.tfi` is an api tree, `.tfs` a component tree (`repository/ProjectProperties.java:319,323`).
187	
188	The cache directories and who writes them: `analyzed_cache` (shared front-end results, `Shell.java:74-75`), `interpreter_parsed_cache` (the interpreter's own analysis cache, `Shell.java:76-77,619`), `interpreter_cache` (the lexically-annotated component, `interpreter/env/ComponentWrapper.java:96`), `environment_cache` (ENVGEN, dead), `bytecode_cache` (jars, `NamingCzar.java:132`), `nativewrapper_cache` (`NamingCzar.java:134`), `optimizedbytecode_cache` (the standalone optimizer), `presyntax_cache` and `syntax_cache` (declared, never used).
189	
190	Staleness is decided by file dates alone (`GraphRepository.java:359-398,526-661`), which is why an edit that does not change a date, or a cache written under a different library world, silently wins.
191	
192	## B.11 The runtime
193	
194	`MainWrapper.main` loads the named class through `InstantiatingClassloader.ONLY` and invokes its no-argument `main` (`runtimeSystem/MainWrapper.java:19,60-67`); program arguments are stashed in a static field rather than passed (`:65`).
195	
196	`InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178`) is where compiled Fortress stops being ordinary bytecode: a class name is examined for markers, and depending on what it finds the loader *generates* the class rather than reading it.
197	
198	It generates: tuple and arrow RTTI classes, closure classes, arrow interfaces and their abstract and wrapped forms, tuple types, union types, and — the general case — an instantiation of a generic template, by reading the template's bytes and rewriting them with ASM through `Instantiater` and an `InstantiationMap` (`:210-290,376-406`, `runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:17-54`).
199	
200	Instantiation renames; it does not change representation. `Instantiater.visit` substitutes type names in the class name, superclass and interfaces (`Instantiater.java:40-54`).
201	
202	The names it matches on are the oxford-bracket and mangled forms defined in `runtimeSystem/Naming.java` (1,203 lines).
203	
204	Tasks: a compiled program's entry class extends `FortressExecutable`, whose static initializer creates one `FortressTaskRunnerGroup` sized by `FORTRESS_THREADS`, with a spawn threshold and loop chunk read from the environment (`runtimeSystem/FortressExecutable.java:22-56`).
205	
206	Transactions: `BaseTask` carries a transaction and exposes `startTransaction`/`endTransaction`/`inATransaction` as static methods the generated code calls (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:180-260`); `inATransaction` builds its debug string eagerly on every call (`:246-249`), the one-line defect already on record in FACTS.
207	
208	This whole subsystem is duplicated, not shared: `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/` and `interpreter/evaluator/transactions/` are a second, independent implementation of the same two ideas.
209	
210	Two `runtimeSystem` classes are used by the interpreter as well: `ByteCodeWriter` and (indirectly) `SimpleClassLoader`, both from `interpreter/env/ClosureMaker.java:47-50`.
211	
212	## B.12 Native code and Java interop
213	
214	The two worlds bind native code by two mechanisms that share nothing but the word "native".
215	
216	Interpreter: a function whose body is literally `builtinPrimitive("some.java.Class")` is pattern-matched in `NativeApp.checkAndLoadNative` (`interpreter/glue/NativeApp.java:164-215`), and that class — a subclass of `NativeFn0..3`/`NativeMeth0..3` in `interpreter/glue/` — is loaded reflectively and takes the evaluator's boxed `FValue`s directly.
217	
218	There are 231 such bindings in `LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss`, 108 in `Library/FortressLibrary.fss` and 7 in `LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss`.
219	
220	Compiler: a `.fss` writes `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{class.method => name, …}` (16 such lines in `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, 3 in `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`); `ForeignJava` reads the Java class with ASM to synthesize an api for it (`repository/ForeignJava.java:132-136,565-575`), and `FortressTransformer` rewrites the class into a wrapper whose methods take and return the compiled world's boxed values (`compiler/nativeInterface/FortressTransformer.java:37`, wrapper written to `nativewrapper_cache` at `:33`).
221	
222	`import java` also works on the interpreter path, by a third route that is easy to miss: `ForeignComponentWrapper` populates an environment from `ForeignJava`'s synthesized declarations (`interpreter/env/ForeignComponentWrapper.java:59`), and `ClosureMaker` generates, at run time, a `NativeFn<n>` subclass that calls the Java method and writes it into `bytecode_cache` (`interpreter/env/ClosureMaker.java:44-50,52`).
223	
224	No test under `ProjectFortress/tests/` uses `import java` (0 files), while 2 under `compiler_tests/` do, so the interpreter's foreign-Java route is present but not exercised by the gated suite.
225	
226	There is no way for a Fortress program to be called *from* Java other than by loading the generated classes through `InstantiatingClassloader`, which is what `MainWrapper` does.
227	
228	## B.13 Where each library enters
229	
230	Interpreter: `default_library` is `AnyType`, `FortressLibrary`, `FortressBuiltin` (`compiler/WellKnownNames.java:48-49,128-137`); the sources are found on `fortress.source.path`, which is `.` then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` then `Library` then `ProjectFortress/test_library` (`default_repository/configuration:44`); they enter as graph roots (`GraphRepository.java:125-165`) and are analysed through the same phase chain as the user program, then linked by `Driver.evalComponent` (`interpreter/Driver.java:140-162`).
231	
232	Compiler: the same source path and the same roots, but `useCompilerLibraries` repoints the names to `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `AnyType` (`WellKnownNames.java:113-126`), and `Types.useCompilerLibraries` repoints the checker's well-known types (`Shell.java:376`).
233	
234	At `fortress run` time the library is not sources at all but jars: `bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar` and friends, found through `bin/run_classpath:26`; if they are absent the class loader falls back to the frozen stubs compiled from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/*.java` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`, which is the misleading-`NoSuchMethodError` trap already on record (`repo-internals.md:165-182`).
235	
236	`LibraryBuiltin` is shared by both worlds in the sense that the directory holds both builtins and `AnyType.fss`, which both use.

238	## B.14 Where the paths diverge, in one table
239	
240	| Concern | Interpreter | Compiler |
241	|---|---|---|
242	| Entry | `Shell.walk` → `Shell.eval` → `Driver` | `Shell.compilerPhases` → `GraphRepository` → `CodeGen`; then a second JVM, `MainWrapper` |
243	| Phases 1-4 | identical | identical |
244	| Integer-literal folding | absent | present (`PhaseOrder.java:141`) |
245	| Type checking | phase present, flag off (`Shell.java:1275`) | on (`Shell.java:405`) |
246	| Desugaring | coercion + getter/setter only | also case, typecase, type ascription, abstract marking |
247	| Overload rewrite | candidates from the disambiguator | candidates from the checker |
248	| Extra phase before execution | lexical-depth rewrite (`interpreter/rewrite/`) | codegen (`compiler/codegen/`) |
249	| Linking | by hand in `Driver.evalComponent` | classpath, plus `linker/` aliases |
250	| Values | `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FFloat`, `FInt`, …) | `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FRR64`, `FZZ32`, …) |
251	| Generics | run-time type objects in `evaluator/types/` | bytecode stamped out at class load by `InstantiatingClassloader` |
252	| Tasks | `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/` | `runtimeSystem/` |
253	| Transactions | `interpreter/evaluator/transactions/` | `runtimeSystem/Transaction.java` |
254	| Natives | `builtinPrimitive` + `interpreter/glue/` | `import java` + `nativeHelpers/` + `nativeInterface/` |
255	| Prelude | `FortressLibrary` (4,518 lines) + `FortressBuiltin` (701) | `CompilerLibrary` (592) + `CompilerBuiltin` (1,547) |
256	
257	Modules on neither path at all: `fib_tests`, `compiler/optimization`, `compiler/environments`, `compiler/asmbytecodeoptimizer`, `parser_util/instrumentation`, `repository/JavaDBRepository` (A.5).

<!-- Territory map, part two: the specification chapter by chapter, and where each feature it defines is implemented on each of the five paths (parser, static checker, interpreter, code generator, compiler prelude). Written before the historical source tree is opened for modification. Every checkable claim cites file:line in this tree; ledger rows are cited by number from explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md. Read with explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, which this document extends and, in two places marked below, corrects. -->

# Specification to implementation

Part one of the map, `explorations/coordinator/map/modules-and-phases.md`, covers the modules and the two pipelines; this part covers the specification and where each feature it defines is implemented. Where the two overlap (the dead top-level `CompilerLibrary/`, the prelude switch in `WellKnownNames`, the phase order) they were written independently and agree.

## 1. The specification that counts

The latest committed specification is `Specification/`; its root is `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex`, a `book` whose seven `\part` files are `\input` at `fortress.tex:149-155`.

The title block reads "Working Draft … July 19, 2012" (`Specification/fortress/fortress.tex:110-116`) and the macro header carries `\def\svnrevision{$Revision: 4267 $}` (`fortress.tex:14`).

The document is 53 numbered chapters plus ten appendices; the built table of contents is `Specification/fortress/fortress.toc` (untracked build residue, from the revival's own LaTeX run, commit `414b790e3`), whose last entry is page 596.

### 1.2 How it differs in scope from `Specification-1.0-frozen/`

At chapter level it does not differ at all: both trees `\input` the same seven parts, the same chapter files, and the same section files, and the set of `\chapter{}` titles in the two trees is identical.

Both trees carry 208 tracked files; 202 are byte-identical, five differ, and one is present only in the frozen tree (`Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf`).

The five differences are: `fortress/fortress.tex` (the revival restyled the authors' `\note`/`\marginnote` macros, commit `4672b71cd`, and fixed the title's date line); the three `fortress/*.pl` table generators (the same commit changed `>>` to `>` so the reserved-word tables are not doubled); and `basic-lib/objects.tex`, where the draft tree carries a stray `\tracingcommands=1\tracingmacros=1` at `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:17`, historical, not a revival edit.

Both roots carry the same `\def\svnrevision{$Revision: 4267 $}` and the same `\ifrelease` block, and in both the release switch is commented out (`Specification/fortress/fortress.tex:33`, `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/fortress.tex:33`), so both build in draft mode with the 230 `\note{}` implementers' annotations rendered.

So the difference in scope is between the *frozen PDF* and the sources, not between the two source trees: `Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf` is a 262-page committed artefact of the 1.0 release, while the sources in both trees build to about 596 pages.

This sharpens, and in one respect corrects, `FACTS.md`'s line "The in-repo `Specification/` is the later draft with the implementers' notes; `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is 1.0": the *sources* under `Specification-1.0-frozen/` are not the 1.0 sources, only the PDF beside them is.

The practical consequence for the ledger's convention ("the chapters cited are byte-identical in `Specification-1.0-frozen`", ledger header) is that the convention holds for 171 of the 173 tracked `.tex` files and fails only for `basic-lib/objects.tex` (by one line) and the root `fortress.tex`.

## 2. How to read the implementation columns

Five paths carry a feature, and a feature can exist on some and not others.

**parser** — the Rats! grammar under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/parser/`; the root module is `Fortress.rats` (179 lines, module assembly only), and the rules live in the 25 modules it instantiates; `templateparser/`, `preparser/` and `import_collector/` are three further grammars serving syntax abstraction, import discovery and dependency collection.

**checker** — `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/`; `typechecker/STypeChecker.scala` plus the four mixins the dispatcher in `typechecker/impls/Dispatch.scala:59-99` routes to (`Decls.scala`, `Functionals.scala`, `Operators.scala`, `Misc.scala`), the standalone checkers beside them, and `overloading/`.

**interpreter** — `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/`; declarations are bound by `evaluator/BuildEnvironments.java`, expressions are walked by `evaluator/Evaluator.java`, and `rewrite/DesugarerVisitor.java` runs an interpreter-only desugaring before evaluation; the library it stands on is `Library/*.fss` plus `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`.

**codegen** — `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java` (6,750 lines), with `compiler/OverloadSet.java` for dispatch methods, `compiler/NamingCzar.java` for type lowering, and `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java` + `Naming.java` for generic instantiation at class-load time; `CodeGen.defaultCase` (`CodeGen.java:1668-1670`) throws `Can't compile <node>` (`sayWhat`, `CodeGen.java:1550-1552`) for every AST node with no `forX` method, so "no visitor" means "absent on this path".

**prelude** — the compiler's own library, selected by `compiler/WellKnownNames.java:113-126` (`useCompilerLibraries()`), is exactly three apis: `CompilerLibrary` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` 592 lines, `.fsi` 307), `CompilerBuiltin` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` 1,547 lines, `.fsi` 754) and `AnyType` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss` 17 lines); `CompilerAlgebra` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss` 29 lines) is commented out of that list at `WellKnownNames.java:118` but reached transitively (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:14`), and `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` (22 lines) must be imported by name.

Two compiler-world files ship and are wired to nothing: `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` (469 lines: the whole generator/reduction protocol in compiler-world spelling) is imported by no prelude file and is named only by a fallback search in `scala_src/typechecker/TraitTable.scala:56-58`; and the top-level `CompilerLibrary/` directory (10 `.fsi` stubs, 3,206 lines, including a 2,523-line `FortressLibrary.fsi`) is not on `fortress.source.path` (`default_repository/configuration`, `fortress.source.path=;.;${_fr}/LibraryBuiltin;${FORTRESS_AUTOHOME}/Library;${_fr}/test_library`) and is referenced by no build file, script or source; the single `bin/` hit for the name, `bin/runOptCollect:32`, is the bytecode-cache jar `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, which is the compiled form of `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and a different thing. The revival-era root `README.md:155` nevertheless describes the directory as "API stubs for the compiler path", which reads as though it were live.

The interpreter's prelude is the other three: `FortressLibrary` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss` 4,518 lines), `FortressBuiltin` and `AnyType` (`WellKnownNames.java:47-48`, `useFortressLibraries()` at `:128-137`).

Two structural facts govern the whole table.

Both paths share one phase list up to DESUGAR and differ only after it (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java:124-145`: `interpreterPhaseOrder` ends in `OVERLOADREWRITE_FOR_INTERPRETER`, `compilerPhaseOrder` in `OVERLOADREWRITE, CODEGEN`), so a feature desugared before that point exists identically on both paths.

`walk` calls `setScala(false)` (`Shell.java:422`) and never `setTypeChecking(true)`, so on the interpreter path the checker is a no-op *and* three desugarings are switched off, each gated on `use_scala`: coercion (`Shell.java:280-282`), chained comparison (`Shell.java:284-286`) and compound/tuple assignment with subscript rewriting (`Shell.java:268-270`).

Status words: **interp** and **comp** each read `works` / `partial` / `absent`, and "absent" on the compiler path most often means the code generator has no visitor or the prelude has no declaration, not that codegen is wrong.

usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full stop
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md; exactly one must, else the
                         nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them

## Execution model

- Two execution paths share parser and phases and differ at the end: the walk interpreter (`fortress file.fss`) and the bytecode compiler (`fortress compile` + `run`) (`repo-internals.md:95-129`).
- The static type checker (Scala, `scala_src/typechecker/`) runs only on the compile path; `walk` turns it off and there is no switch to make it run in the interpreter (`repo-internals.md:127`); every "type error" seen from the interpreter is a run-time dispatch failure.
- `fortress typecheck` checks against `Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`, not the interpreter's prelude, so it is not an oracle for interpreter programs (ledger row 69); making the checker usable on interpreter programs means giving it the interpreter's prelude, which is not a ledger row and not on the worklist as a separate item (it falls under worklist item 2, compiler-path library parity).
- The code generator lowers every type to a JVM reference type: `RR64` to the runtime class `FRR64`, no `dadd`/`dmul` anywhere in the generated loop (shown in bytecode, `perf-probes/boxing/javap/`); arrays are library objects over `get`/`put`, not `double[]` (`repo-internals.md:129`).
- On microGPT-shaped array code boxing is the dominant representational cost, 6.3× (dot product), 6.5× (matrix product) and 2.6× (row lift) over `double[]` in Java models of the program's three kernels, and nothing microGPT-shaped compiles: the compiler prelude lacks the array types, with `Array`, `Vector` and `Array3` undefined in `FlatArrays.fsi` (row 305, wider than row 72). On the interpreter, the only path that runs the kernels, 43.5% is the AST walk, 32.3% environment lookup, 5.2% type dispatch and 0% number representation (JFR on `krows`). The two one-line runtime defects the probe found are fixed (rows 302, 303; the next two entries), and no array type goes into the compiler prelude: the arrays reach the compiled path with the one library (POSITIONS, the library route). A failed compile leaves a 0-byte jar in the bytecode cache (`perf-probes/kernels/REPORT.md`).
- The boxing probe's scalar-loop reading, 156× primitive Java with boxing about 2% of it, is of the tree before rung 0's two fixes (rows 302, 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`); of the costs it named, `countedseqloop`'s boxed indices and closure call (about 7%) and the representational rest (about 30%) are unaddressed (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- The eager debug string of `BaseTask.inATransaction()` is fixed: the message is built only under the `debug` flag (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:248`; row 302; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `FFloatLiteral`'s String round trip is fixed: the literal caches its `double` instead of re-parsing its text in `asRR64()` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/runtimeValues/FFloatLiteral.java`; row 303; `compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- The benchmark numbers on record from 2026-09-15 (`bench1t` 9.3441 s, `bench1h` 6.0732 s) were taken on a quieter machine: the same unmodified tree measured 13.0566 s and 8.8159 s in another session, so absolute seconds are not comparable across sessions and only a before/after pair taken in one session is (`compile-ladder/rung0/REPORT.md`).
- `ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars: the first `fortress compile` after a rebuild of the compiler clears `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/`, and `fortress run` then dies with `NoClassDefFoundError: fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`; the library-order recompile of `repo-internals.md:170-179` restores it, about two minutes.
- The compiled path's bytecode cache can come up empty after a library-order rebuild that reports exit 0; re-running the same commands one at a time produced the jars (`perf-probes/boxing/REPORT.md`).
- Generic instantiations are stamped out at class-load time by ASM rewriting of template bytecode (`InstantiatingClassloader.java`, `repo-internals.md:129`); a size is in the stamped class's name (`pNatMeth$Box⟦3⟧`, `perf-probes/nat/java.md` § 1; `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md`), and its descriptor in a stamped class is `RTTIsize.of("<n>")` ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics).
- Implicit parallelism: `for` is parallel unless every generator is `seq`; the elements of a tuple and the operands of an operator are evaluated in parallel implicit threads (`tuple-expr.tex:23-24`, `operator-app.tex:59`; row 265). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sizes the work-stealing pool; there is no explicit threading in any of our programs.
- The compile path's checker cannot check `nat` parameters at all (see "The checker and the one library" below): this no longer holds. The checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters ("The compiled type checker checks `nat` and `int` static parameters" below), and a sized program loads and runs compiled ("A size is carried at run time as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`" under Landed semantics). Sizes in types (`nat` parameters) are "instantiated at runtime" by the specification (`trait-parameters.tex`, natparams); they check shapes when a value is made or passed; no optimization is built on them anywhere. A `nat`-typed parameter does not unify statically with a run-time-built array (row 23); the interpreter matches at dispatch, and a mismatch reads "Failed to find any matching overload", uncatchable (row 83). A literal size does unify (row 23's positive half).

<!-- What Pavol has decided, holds or already knows, as it stands now: each position in plain words, what we do and why, under a bold title that is its handle; a quote only where his words are the position itself. Timeless: no dates, no provenance, no account of how a position was reached. That record is `POSITIONS-history.md`, where every earlier text of every entry stands verbatim with what became of it. A position he has replaced is gone from here and the later one stands; a decision not yet built keeps the detail the coming work needs. A worker or a coordinator may add an entry with a date or a quote in it; the next consolidation compiles that out into the history and leaves the position. Standing directives about how we work are in `explorations/protocol.md`, and what is established is in `FACTS.md`; neither is repeated here. Read whole at session start, so that none of it is re-asked or re-explained. -->

# Pavol's positions, decisions and known ground

## The goal

- **The measuring stick.** Finish what the designers intended, judged by the specification in `Specification/`, the Working Draft of 2010-12 as the revival revises it, with the 2012 Types chapter cited beside it; not redesign the language. The measure is one program, microGPT, compiled to bytecode and running fast. A pure-Java microGPT is written later as the floor to measure against. The specification is a living document that reflects the changes we make. The tree is tagged `sealed-tree` at the map's last commit; commits after it edit the original sources, test-driven.
- **How he weighs his calls where the designers left no word.** "I don't care about type theoretical purity and I'm accepting all unfinished corners of the language because I want to get to a compiled version of micro GPT. And I think this is the right pragmatic approach so that we do not get bogged down in weeds. Theory. We want to get this one program running fast. That's our guiding star. But along the way, I want to stay true to the spirit of Fortress." He has not read the specification, the papers on its type system or the library, and relies on the record: "I assume those people knew much more than I do right now." The check he asked for is a thorough top-tier review of every decision of his against the designers' intent, for errors of commission and of omission (`reviews/decisions-review/evidence.md`, `judgement.md`, `popl-recheck.md`); its items are decisions below.
- **The readable expression.** The toy problem is microGPT and the search is for its most readable expression: "we are searching for the optimal expression of the microGPT algorithm for readability." Fortress's mathematical notation and Iverson's APL notation (with Hsu's data design for data-flow algorithms) are the two sources. The Hsu-style flat program gave "a few lumps of coal", not a diamond; the vocabulary is where any polishing happens. C4 is the APL target form; C2's tuple hyperparameter form is what a strand assignment expands to; the semicolon form is set aside.
- **The APL side quest is closed.** It was a curiosity, then a ladder to learn APL, then native code (not an interpreter in an interpreter) with microGPT as its target; its remaining ground (tacit, characters, nested arrays) is not pursued.
- **The 2D notation is a gimmick.** Fortify's mathematical rendering is "a neat gimmick, not a good idea": it encodes one perspective on a computation into the syntax, while the same mathematics can be written many ways; APL's glyph-per-transformation is the purer realisation. Presentation only, not on the path, not an argument for Fortress; no work on it unless he asks.
- **The type checker on interpreter programs.** He wants the checker, which runs only on the compile path, usable on interpreter programs, and considers it low-hanging fruit. It comes after the switch-over, when walk also takes the static coercions the checker inserts (the entry on walk's choice of coercions).

## History he knows (do not re-explain)

- **The project's end.** DARPA's HPCS did not take Sun into phase three (2006) and the project lived on at Sun Labs until 2012. His reading: they did no work on performance, "mucked around with syntax", and the promise that a sufficiently advanced compiler would later make mathematical types fast was never true; the funding was pulled for good reason.
- **Boxed numerics.** The compiled path is only about ten times the interpreter because numerics are boxed (`FRR64`, no `DADD`); "without unboxed doubles and arrays of doubles, what are we even doing here". The first measurement's scalar loop was an edge case microGPT never hits (literals in the loop, a `:=` accumulator); the fairer test he asked for agreed with him (FACTS § Execution model). The storage is his decision below; unboxed arithmetic is phase 6 of the plan.
- **Hsu's critique** of language paradigms as accidental complexity; he is "coming around to his point of view".
- **The third-party Java 9 port** gets no credit and no mention: "I don't wanna see them mentioned anywhere." CLAUDE.md no longer describes the tree as the port's migration grafted on the history; the other files that repeat that sentence wait for the lineage cleanup (`PLAN.md`). His plan to rename the graft-free `clean-ladder` branch to `main` was not carried out.

## Decisions on record

### The standard and the sources

- **The specification stays the standard, the Types chapter beside it.** Where the Types chapter of the team's unfinished restart (`Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`) covers a topic, it is cited beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word: the exclusion rule as "instantiation exclusion" in its two-part form, the `covariant` modifier, `Bottom` inexpressible. "On the rule S revises, it is the designers' latest intent, and the goal is to finish what they intended."
- **The type group's late positions outweigh the early text.** The specification "was written in a vacuum early on", "as a wish"; "then the type group went in and tried to make it run. So they knew much more about what's feasible and what's not. The goal was performance. The specialization is a must"; "when that wish met reality, then the spec must change"; "whatever the spec was dreaming about in 2008 is irrelevant because it met hard reality". So the late, implementation-informed positions of the type group (the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the compiled tower flattened by Steele in 2011, Naden's 2012 write-up, the POPL 2019 paper) outweigh the specification's earlier text where they conflict, and the implementers' later word outweighs unfinished text. "We are not Naden. We know nothing here."
- **The library's own practice is the standard.** "all the extensions that [microGPT] invented need to go directly to the standard library in the spirit of the standard library." Exclusion "is a practice that is all over the standard library"; whoever extends the library "should study the existing parts of the Fortress library meticulously, and use those patterns for extending the standard library in the native way". No fix is designed from a reading of the specification alone or from a user-side workaround. A fork put to him names the library's own way first, and a fork resting on a rule that refuses something says what the library does instead (protocol principle 2). The lesson behind the rule: he had to find the diagonal's override shape himself ("why the fuck did I have to invent this solution?"), because the step skipped was what the library already does in the same family.
- **Fleshing out the standard library** is a very important task: first the `RR64`/`AdditiveGroup` mismatch (done by the flattening), then the algebraic layer (Ring, Field and what ML's matrices and tensors need) so the library's trait flavour reaches them; into the standard library itself, not a tree of our own.
- **Interpreter performance is irrelevant.** "interpreter of Fortress, which is hundreds times slower than the Python interpreter, is irrelevant for any performance discussions"; "we cannot judge anything performance related in Fortress while we do not have a compiler". No edit to C4 for speed, and no performance decision of any kind until microGPT runs compiled. The two microGPT programs never run in the gate ("those are too long running to be tests"); the ladder-regression stage compiles them and records the phase; when they one day run, the run goes to a separate non-gating stage.
- **Development-loop performance is a first-class concern.** When an iteration waits too long on something, find the cause and fix it.
- **The territory map** (`coordinator/map/`) is the map down to where the design intent is written, papers as well as the specification; he wanted it before unsealing. The maps exist so that nothing on record is rediscovered; the boot order is followed as written, `INDEX.md` included.
- **The plan** (`coordinator/PLAN.md`) is six phases, approved with its workers: 1, the wrapping operators, the specification rung without the number chapters and the run-time size rung; 2, the flattening, the number chapters and the overflow natives; 3, the checker at a true zero; 4, the switch-over, natives then names; 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code-generation holes; 6, microGPT fast. Phases 1 and 2 are landed. His answers come in the plan's order; the re-approval rows and the other off-path items are parked until relevant; row 41 joins the switch-over's design.

### The one library and the compiled checker

- **The library route.** "we need to unify this. into single library"; "the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it." One library, the interpreter's (`FortressLibrary` + `FortressBuiltin`), becomes the library the compiler checks; no declaration goes into the compiler's prelude (`CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra`); the prelude-name rungs of the ladder stopped, code-generator rungs continue; the three prelude files are deleted at the switch-over and their tests kept. How the checker is brought to accept the library is a plan put to him step by step, not a decision to re-ask.
- **The compiler prelude's leftovers go at the switch-over.** The compiler-prelude block for `Maybe` stands as landed, its tests kept, its lines gone then; the guard `if other = -1 then 0` in the two compiled `REM` bodies (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss:601`, `:686`) stays and goes with the prelude; the prelude's reversed spellings of the wrapping and saturating operators (row 348) are respelled then, in 10 compiled test files; `ZZ64`'s compiled shift declaration (row 381) closes when the compiled path reads this library; the specification's `shift` (row 383) reaches the compiled path then, `compiler_tests/XXXShiftDeclRungI.test` promoted and `shift` a reserved name on the compiled path from then on, the switch-over batch measuring which compiler tests bind it.
- **The checker count is measured, never red.** The checker-count stage stays in every gate, reported and never red on its own; the full distance measurement (all apis and components) is a report-only stage of the phase-3 gates, whose job is driving it down.
- **Sizes.** The checker checks `nat` and `int` parameters (built). A size left unknown after inference is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value, and nothing otherwise ("the middle is a clear winner"); how the checker represents an unknown size was not his to decide. Deleting the dead sizes (E3, 25 api declarations) is shown to him as a diff with the switch-over's design, with row 41. Every static argument counts in the exclusion rule except operator arguments ("sizes count"); booleans follow once the checker supports boolean parameters (row 406). A size the call cannot fix is an error at that call, also inside overload sets: when the arm the rules would pick has a size the call cannot fix, the call is refused with the same "could not infer" error instead of the arm being dropped (row 400 closed). A `nat` parameter is an `NN32` value and an `int` parameter a `ZZ32` (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:82-90`); a larger one is refused; the array design refuses a JVM array length over 2^31-1 where it makes storage ("that's not even a question"). A size used as a value converts to `ZZ32` as a numeral does (row 485); sizes as `NN32` and ranges as `ZZ32` are consistent, since array lengths and indices are Java `int`, a size is never negative and ranges count through negatives. All built.
- **The run-time size design is B.** A size at run time gets the same descriptor object a type argument has, filling the slot the team's code generator reserved ("of course, let's extend the runtime object with a new field for the size"); one descriptor per number from a table, no holder class, the team's instantiation pattern applied to numbers. Operators are not unified with the descriptor-bearing kinds ("I don't see a need"). Built.
- **The implicit bound of an unbounded type parameter is `Any`**, the top, holding tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not; the library's generic containers are instantiated at tuples, arrays indexed by pairs among them. The specification states it (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:49-62`), with a callout recording the Working Draft's `Object` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex:49-50`) and naming the compile path's `Object` setting (row 412) as the divergence until the switch-over.
- **The exclusion rule stays and the tower is flat (route A).** "Agreed. Route A it is." The compiled checker keeps the multiple instantiation exclusion rule; the library's numeric tower is flattened as Steele flattened the compiler prelude in 2011: the fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` siblings under `Number`, each carrying its own algebra, `Number` without its catch-all operators, a `coerce` on each wider type converting from the narrower; the interpreter converts by coercion at dispatch; the specification is revised with a decision record that preserves the original text, the reasoning and route C. ℤ sits inside ℚ by coercion. Built. Reversal to route C costs what FACTS's route C entry lists. His readings while the fork was open stand: the patents' forest rule against the flattened prelude was "the team's last record on how to do the 'Fortress' way", the route culminating in the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule and specialisation by a run-time return-type check; and "without specialized code there will be no change at performance. But how a specialization is chosen 'ist mir egal', as long as it runs fast."
- **`AnyIntegral`'s closure and how the checker reads `comprises`.** The generic scalar-extension block with its two unnamed choices, the `AnyAdditiveGroup` marker and the `Array3` exclusion stand as landed, and so does the closure `AnyIntegral comprises { ... }`, with a `NOT YET`-style comment in the team's wording at the line. The checker reads a `comprises` clause the 2012 way (the later Types chapter, `types.tick:384-389`, and Welterweight): a generic child of a closed trait is eligible when every type the checker knows under it is listed (`everyKnownSubtypeListed`), with an S1 callout in `Specification/basic/traits.tex`; the clause and walk stay as they are; a ledger row records the hole every way but the 2008 clause shares (a program's own `Integral` subtype in another component is not caught). Built. Of the api's overloading and return-type errors this let through, answer 9's families are repaired by the library's own exclusions, `seq`'s remaining pairs aside (FACTS, "The one library's refused overload families are repaired by its own exclusions ..."), and the meet rule and the residue are batch 8's.
- **The static-parameter sentence goes (answer 9).** The specification's sentence that overloads may not differ in static parameters is dropped; the specification is revised to the type group's 2011 model the checker runs, the original kept as superseded text in the S1 form. The checker keeps the paper's three rules with two changes: the return-type rule is checked over every instance, and one narrow rule stays, that two generic arms in the more-specific relation agree on their static parameters position by position (Java's overriding rule; it closes row 398). Walk dispatches by declared domains, which ends its dependence on declaration order. The library's refused families are repaired by its own devices. No model line changes. Built: the specification states the 2011 model; the checker checks the return-type rule over every instance, and the positional rule, return-type condition only, for two declarations with as many static parameters of their own, the scope listed for his review; walk chooses by declared domains; the library's families are repaired by its own exclusions but for `seq`'s remaining pairs (FACTS, "The specification states the type group's 2011 overloading model ...", "The compiled checker checks the Return Type Rule over every instance and answer 9's positional rule", "Walk chooses between a generic declaration and another on their declared domains ..." and "The one library's refused overload families are repaired by its own exclusions ..."). The judgement's
- **Conversions never change which declaration runs.** A conversion is applied to make a call possible and never changes which declaration runs when one already fits; declarations are chosen by the coercion chapter's order, applicability and specificity taken on declared, quantified domains as answer 9 words them (a generic declaration fits when some instance within its bound fits); the chosen declaration is then instantiated by answer 8's promotion, its coercions inserted statically, and the rewritten call dispatches on the converted values; a numeral whose candidate types are incomparable reads as `ZZ32` (`ZZ64` or `ZZ` by magnitude), stated once in the inference chapter. So a generic arm over `T extends Number` beside a plain arm over `Any` runs the generic at `ZZ64` for a mixed-width call, the specialised instance; plain declarations are untouched; the broader rule (his own idea, "if there is a conversion to a specific type, it should be applied. And only if all combinations are exhausted and we haven't reached a specific implementation, then we go to a plain implementation") is not taken. His principle behind it: "we must make it fast, and generic is never fast. So make it fast." — fast code a JVM can specialise. With it, the inference rule: the checker infers a static argument with coercion, answer 8's promotion its number case, and keeps the expected type at a call written `f(x)` with a retry without it, so that a binding's coercion still applies; walk does the same 
- **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`** (row 484), as `QQ`, `RR64`, the compiler library and the specification's `ZZ` do, so under walk the family answers at the promoted type. Built.
- **A type parameter the arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom` (the paper's instance rule).** From the POPL 2019 paper (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, "Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance", `research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`; the authors could not prove the value's rule and replaced it, pp. 11:19, 11:25): such a parameter takes the intersection of its upper bounds, its declared bound (`Any` if none) under the constraint of the call's static return type; never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, never the value's type alone. "if I apply the rule that the ... later teams work supersedes the previous one, and you are saying the rule is coming from the paper and it helps us cleanly resolve something, then I will trust the team's work over whatever my misunderstanding of the things are." Which declaration runs stays the conversion rule above. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, so it is unaffected. Built in the specification: the dispatch paragraph and the inference chapter state the rule, with a callout that both implementations take the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter, walk by necessity (it has no static types) and the compiled path until phase 5 (FACTS, "The specification gives the run-time instance of a dispatched declaration by the POPL 2019 paper's rule ..."); the recheck's smaller sentences are in as defaults, listed for his review. Walk keeps row 157's fix as its best; the compiled path's departure is g
- **The order of the checker's attempts at a call** (row 508): the checker tries a call by subtyping without the expected type first and keeps that attempt when its result converts to the expected type, then tries coercion with the context, so a declaration that fits the arguments as they are is not passed over for one reached by coercion. One checker rung in batch 8; `XXXInferContextKeepsFit` promoted.
- **Walk chooses coercions on the value, for now.** Walk has no static types, so it chooses a coercion on the value where the specification's coercion chapter and the compiled path resolve it statically (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:619-662`; `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`); accepted as the interpreter's limit, stated in one S1 callout at that passage (`:663-675`); item 16 is closed with those two tests as its record. Walk is made to match after the switch-over, once the checker runs on interpreter programs and walk takes the static coercions the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, so the two paths agree on it.
- **The `comprises` passages read at the level of values (PLAN item 26, row 491).** The four passages of the specification that read a `comprises` clause at the level of types are restated at the level of values, "covers" is defined once, the Meet Rule has the closed-trait case, and row 492 is repaired on both paths; the proof appendix keeps its existence lemmas and gives up static uniqueness for run-time uniqueness, a call whose argument's static type sits between typed by the intersection of its candidates' return types. Built (FACTS, "The specification gives the run-time instance of a dispatched declaration ...", "The compiled checker accepts the Meet Rule's `comprises` example by a coverage check local to overload checking ..." and "Walk's load check reads a generic declaration beside a plain one on declared domains ..."). The separate analysis session's proof addendum (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md`, written at his request: he was "super scared that we are touching type theoretical things that I am totally unequipped to handle") has three points built in: Fortress already dispatches at run time with one static winner, so the performance cost claimed for such calls is unproven; the coverage search stays local to overload checking and does not widen assignment or ordinary subtyping; the proof holds only where closed families are closed, which row 487 leaves unenforced across some component boundaries. Its acceptance pair is gated as written (`CoverageRetu
- **The separate analysis session's scope.** Its contributions are reviews and their documentation commits on a branch of their own from `main`, not an implementation batch or a change to the agreed route.
- **The `covariant` keyword is future work**, not on the path to microGPT. Row 404 records the soundness hole: the checker accepts variance and neither path carries it to run time; its expected-failure tests are owed in a batch rung. Worklist item 12 is declaration-site variance by the keywords, carried to run time on both paths. When covariance lands, "resurrect" the specification's sign-refined number types as covariant static parameters (the note's way 2, probe `Q3Phantom`); the specification's superseded-design note points to that road.

### Numbers

- **The integer principle.** "we should use Java or JVM defaults where it makes sense, but we shouldn't be shy to correct the mistakes of JVM when seen through the lens of high performance and mathematical precision language", as the designers did with rounding and the sign of `GCD`; "they were running on JVM is basically an accident of history, a bootstrap"; "high performance languages should give you tools to stay close to the metal … Swift and Rust type of reasoning": where hardware behaviour is expressible in bytecode it gets its own explicit spelling, in the family the specification already has for wrapping and saturating; "if the JVM itself is precluding such implementation then I guess at this point in time we should just give up fighting with the JVM". Julia and X10 are the counterparts to compare, beside Swift and Rust.
- **`round` on an exact half goes to the even integer** on both paths, the specification's rule for rationals, IEEE's default and the team's own rational body. Built.
- **`floor` and `ceiling` on the float types keep the float** (row 330): "So floor returns float." The brackets ⌊x⌋ and ⌈x⌉, `round` and `truncate` return the unbounded ℤ, and the library's spellings of `truncate` and `round` are tidied to the same. A library rung after the switch-over, gated, with the count of interpreter tests whose output changes measured first.
- **`LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` are bit operators; `shift` is exact on ℤ** (row 335). On the fixed widths `LSHIFT`/`RSHIFT` are bit operators with the smart-shift rule, since every peer language lets shifted-out bits fall silently ("if every other language does something else, that's the clearest red flag to stop and pause and reconsider"), and the specification's arithmetic `shift` is exact on ℤ. His reservation for the code generator: on the fixed widths the compiled code shifts the machine word, never through ℤ. Built on both paths; `shift` reaches the compiled path at the switch-over. A `ZZ32` is shifted by a count of any integral width (rows 380, 381): `ZZ32`'s shift pair is declared with any integral count, as `Integral[\I\]` promises and as `ZZ`, `NN64` and `ZZ64`'s implementation do, `ZZ64`'s api lines matching its implementation; built under walk, the compiled side at the switch-over.
- **`GCD`/`LCM`** (row 334): nonnegative results as the specification says, and an overflow error when the multiple does not fit, on both paths. Built.

Syntactically, a type parameter consists of an identifier followed by an
optional \KWD{extends} clause, followed by an optional
``\EXP{\KWD{absorbs}\;\;\KWD{unit}}'' clause (described in
\secref{absorbing-units}).
If a type parameter does not have an \KWD{extends} clause, it has an
implicit ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}'' clause.
\revision{revival-bound}{The Working Draft of February 2011 gave such a type
parameter the implicit clause ``\EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}}''.
\TYP{Any} holds every value, tuples and \TYP{()} among them, which \TYP{Object}
does not (the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012); \library\ are
written under \TYP{Any}, instantiating such parameters at tuple types, and the
interpreter reads the bound so.
The type group's paper of 2019 says the same: ``By default, each type parameter
has an upper bound Any'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019).
The compiled path still gives such a type parameter of a program's own
declarations the bound \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the revival's gap ledger), a
divergence that lasts until the compiled path is switched over to the
interpreter's library.}

FACTS.md:61
- **A numeral's type depends on the path and on the library in scope, and only `x.one` and the witness `typecase` produce a `T` in generic code on both paths** (`reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/evidence-B.md` §§ 3.1, 4.1, 6.2, probes under `reviews/numerics-plan-coordinator/probes-B/`). The compiled checker types every integer numeral `IntLiteral` and every radix-point numeral `FloatLiteral`, never looking at the value (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:467-473`), resolved in the builtin library in scope (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java:61-62`): with the compiler library a trait that each integer type coerces from (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:390`), with the one library `object IntLiteral extends { ZZ32 }`, its arithmetic withheld "until coercion is implemented" (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:117`, `:125-127`), and `object FloatLiteral extends RR64` (`:44`). Walk makes an integer numeral an `Int`, a `Long` or a `BigNum` by magnitude and a radix-point numeral a `FloatLiteral` below `RR64` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/evaluator/values/FIntLiteral.java:40-56`). The one library's `IntLiteral extends ZZ32` is why a numeral passes to a `ZZ32` parameter of a generic function there (`scaleT(BoxT[\String\](2), 3)`, `probes-B/BGenCk2.check.txt`, a06), which the compiler library, whose `IntLiteral` each integer type coerces from, takes by the checker's inference with coercion (row 401; `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/NatLitArgChecker.fss:16`), and why an untyped `hd = 4` binds `IntLiteral` on the checker and `Int` under walk. At a typed binding `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `RR64` and `QQ` take a numeral on both paths, `NN32` and `NN64` refuse one and `RR32` refuses `1.5` on both (row 454), and `a: ZZ32 = 3000000000` and `a: RR64 = 3000000000` pass the checker, with no range check, and are refused by walk as a `Long` (rows 325, 443). A number of type `T` in generic code: `x + x.one` gives `6 : Long` for a `ZZ64` and `6 : NN32` for an `NN32` under walk and checks, and so does the `() -> T` witness `typecase` with `cast[\T\](widen(1))` branches, whose compiled `cast` matches (row 426, closed with row 351); `cast[\T\](1)` with `T = ZZ64` is a `CastError` under walk (it does not convert), `1 asif T` is refused on both paths, `widen(1)` is right under walk only for `T = ZZ64` and refused by the checker, and a copy of the library's own `__thrower`, `thr[\T\](): T = throw ForbiddenException`, is refused by the checker ("'throw' can only throw objects of Exception type"). A range's components are `ZZ32` in the one library, and under walk a range over another integer type stops at its construction ("The one library's scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` alone" under Landed semantics). Where a numeral's own type lands on each path is the numeral switch (POSITIONS, "The numeral switch, split by where the static types are"; "The numeral switch, measured under walk on the tree after climb batch N ..." below).

(************************************************************
* \subsection*{Numeric hierarchy}
************************************************************)

(** Place holder for exclusions of AdditiveGroup **)
trait AnyAdditiveGroup end

(** Additive group making use of %+%.  Must define %+% and
    either unary or binary %-%. **)
trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends AnyAdditiveGroup
    getter zero(): T
    abstract opr +(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self) : T
end

(** Place holder for exclusions of MultiplicativeRing **)
trait AnyMultiplicativeRing end

(** Multiplicative ring using TIMES and juxtaposition.
    Define opr TIMES; juxtaposition is defined in terms of TIMES. **)
trait MultiplicativeRing[\T extends MultiplicativeRing[\T\]\]
        extends { AdditiveGroup[\T\], AnyMultiplicativeRing }
    abstract getter one(): T
    abstract opr TIMES(self, other:T): T
    opr juxtaposition(self, other:T): T
    (** Exponentiation need only deal with natural exponents. **)
    opr ^(self, other:ZZ64): T
end

trait Number extends { AnyAdditiveGroup, AnyMultiplicativeRing }
        comprises { RR64, RR32, QQ, AnyIntegral, IntLiteral }
    (** The value as a float, the explicit conversion into %RR64%. **)
    asFloat(self): RR64
    (** Two exact numbers of different types compare as rationals; a float
        compares with any number after %asFloat%, so an exact value equals
        its nearest float. **)
    opr =(self, other:Number):Boolean
end

\item
\emph{Loose juxtaposition}, that is, juxtaposition with intervening
whitespace, has higher precedence than any operator listed below.  The
associativity of loose juxtaposition is type-dependent and is
different from that for tight juxtaposition; see \secref{juxtameaning}.
Note that \emph{lopsided juxtaposition}
(having whitespace on one side but not the other) is a static error as
described in \secref{operator-fixity}.


\item
Prefix operators have higher precedence than any operator listed below.
However, it is a static error for an operand of a loose prefix operator
to be an operand of a tight infix operator.

\item
The infix operators are partitioned into certain traditional groups, as
explained below.  They have higher precedence than any operator listed below.

\item
The equal symbol `\EXP{=}' in binding context,
the assignment operator `\EXP{\ASSIGN}', and
compound assignment operators (\EXP{\mathrel{+}=}, \EXP{-=}, \EXP{\wedge=},
\EXP{\vee=}, \EXP{\cap=}, \EXP{\cup=}, and so on as described in
\secref{operator-app-expr})
have lower precedence than any operator listed above.
Note that compound assignment operators themselves are not operator names.

The relational operators are further categorized as equivalence,
inequivalence, ordering, and other.
